title: Waste Books
author: Georg Christoph Lichtenberg
context: Waste Books - by Georg Christoph Lichtenberg Recommend it: 10/10. Date read: 2025-09-03. Tweets from 1765-1799 by a 4’9” hunchback physicist, friends with Goethe and Kant, admired by Nietzsche, Schopenhauer, etc. Such wonderful random thoughts, beautiful perspectives on thinking for yourself, observing nature, language, freedom, philosophy, religion, and more. Hundreds of initial insights, especially inspiring because they’re undeveloped.

title: You Can Negotiate Anything
author: Herb Cohen
context: You Can Negotiate Anything - by Herb Cohen Recommend it: 10/10. Date read: 2023-08-02. Everything is negotiable. Challenge authority. You have the power in any situation. This is how to realize it and use it. A must-read classic from 1980 from a master negotiator. My notes here aren’t enough because the little book is filled with so many memorable stories — examples of great day-to-day moments of negotiation that will stick in your head for when you need them. (I especially loved the one about the power of the prisoner in solitary confinement.) So go buy and read the book. I’m giving it a 10/10 rating even though the second half of the book loses steam, because the first half is so crucial.

title: The Listening Book
author: W.A. Mathieu
context: The Listening Book - by W.A. Mathieu Recommend it: 10/10. Date read: 2021-09-03. Everyone should read this book of little essays about listening. It teaches your ears to pay more attention. It calls your attention to sounds you hadn’t noticed. It’s beautifully written, and makes your life better. I read it twice, 24 years ago, and reading it again this week, it was even better than I remembered.

title: The Courage to Be Disliked
author: Ichiro Kishimi and Fumitake Koga
context: The Courage to Be Disliked - by Ichiro Kishimi and Fumitake Koga Recommend it: 10/10. Date read: 2018-07-25. Wow. A profound little philosophy book from Japan, communicating the psychology of Alfred Adler - a rival of Freud. Told as a conversation between an angry student and a patient teacher. A little book so good that I rushed home from other activities to keep reading it, and finished in a day. A surprisingly fresh perspective on how to live. (The “disliked” part is not the point, so don’t let the title distract you.)

title: Sum: Forty Tales from the Afterlives
author: David Eagleman
context: Sum: Forty Tales from the Afterlives - by David Eagleman Recommend it: 10/10. Date read: 2017-09-27. Awesomely creative think-piece. 40 very short fictional stories about what happens when you die. The framework is inspiring for anyone: coming up with 40 different answers to any one question. But they’re also just brilliant ideas and powerful little fables. I just read it a 2nd time and love it even more now.

title: The Gardener and the Carpenter
author: Alison Gopnik
context: The Gardener and the Carpenter - by Alison Gopnik Recommend it: 10/10. Date read: 2016-08-10. Great philosophy of parenting, from a grandmother who is a wise professor of philosophy and a developmental psychologist. Such a beautiful mindset and outlook. Required reading for every parent. Re-read it often as a necessary reminder.

title: Playful Parenting
author: Lawrence Cohen
context: Playful Parenting - by Lawrence Cohen Recommend it: 10/10. Date read: 2016-06-05. I’ve read many books on parenting, but this one is the best. It’s genius. My top recommendation for everyone with a kid age 1-13. Its point is that children communicate through play. So, to reach them: play! Anything can be done through play: teaching, emotional connection, processing difficult situations, and even discipline can be made playful. Read the whole book instead of just my notes, since my little take-away ideas are just reminders of the spirit of the book. I re-read these notes almost every week to remind me how to be a great parent. My kid is always thankful (communicated through giddy laughter) when I remember and use this approach.

title: On Writing Well
author: William Zinsser
context: On Writing Well - by William Zinsser Recommend it: 10/10. Date read: 2015-08-01. Great blunt advice about writing better non-fiction. So inspiring.

title: The War of Art
author: Steven Pressfield
context: The War of Art - by Steven Pressfield Recommend it: 10/10. Date read: 2012-01-05. Have you experienced a vision of the person you might become, the work you could accomplish, the realized being you were meant to be? Are you a writer who doesn’t write, a painter who doesn’t paint, an entrepreneur who never starts a venture? Then you know what “Resistance” is. This book is about that. Read it.

title: Stumbling on Happiness
author: Daniel Gilbert
context: Stumbling on Happiness - by Daniel Gilbert Recommend it: 10/10. Date read: 2007-07-11. Not at all new-agey, as the title might suggest. Harvard professor of psychology has studied happiness for years, and shares factual findings that will change the way you look at the world.

title: E-Myth Revisited
author: Michael Gerber
context: E-Myth Revisited - by Michael Gerber Recommend it: 10/10. Date read: 2004-02-26. Absolutely everyone who is an entrepreneur or wants to be one needs to read this book. I first read it after 10 years of successfully running my company, and was still blown away and totally humbled by its wisdom. Re-reading it today, I'm amazed how my view of business was completely changed by this one little book. See my notes for examples, but definitely read the book itself to get the real impact.

title: You’re Not Listening
author: Kate Murphy
context: You’re Not Listening - by Kate Murphy Recommend it: 9/10. Date read: 2026-02-25. Being a great listener when people speak. Deep insights about understanding, connection, helping people express themselves, overcoming assumptions, the ethics of gossip, and more. Specific techniques for the support response, encouraging elaboration, and keeping it balanced. You can’t be ethical without being a good listener. When people say, “I can’t talk right now,” what they really mean is “I can’t listen right now.”

title: The Invention of the Jewish People
author: Shlomo Sand
context: The Invention of the Jewish People - by Shlomo Sand Recommend it: 9/10. Date read: 2024-10-10. Fascinating subject. Countries are made of stories. Kings didn’t need their subjects to agree, but nations do. So to build a nation, they need to make a story that helps people feel a shared identity, nationalism, and what distinguishes them from their neighbors. Back-creating a history. Founders of Israel did this brilliantly.

title: Between Us: How Cultures Create Emotions
author: Batja Mesquita
context: Between Us: How Cultures Create Emotions - by Batja Mesquita Recommend it: 9/10. Date read: 2024-04-05. Cultural psychology, studying emotions through the lens of culture. Your emotions are created by your culture. You should not be too sure that you share the emotional experiences of individuals from other cultures. Culture and emotion make each other up. Great insights!

title: China’s World View
author: David Daokui Li
context: China’s World View - by David Daokui Li Recommend it: 9/10. Date read: 2024-03-10. Senior academic advisor to the Chinese Communist Party feels most political tensions come from a misunderstanding of China’s world view, hence the subtitle “demystifying to prevent global conflict”, and his intrinsic desire to explain. I love its insights and historical context, especially around “Respect-centered diplomacy” and how the CCP is structured.

title: Arabs
author: Tim Mackintosh-Smith
context: Arabs - by Tim Mackintosh-Smith Recommend it: 9/10. Date read: 2024-02-03. 3000 years of factual Arab history, and personal insights from this Oxford Brit who lived in Yemen for 37 years, translates classical Arabic, and clearly cares a lot. Huge and thorough but really wonderful for those with the interest. I loved his writing style and poetic asides. Read my notes here for a taste. What a great book.

title: The Vagabond’s Way
author: Rolf Potts
context: The Vagabond’s Way - by Rolf Potts Recommend it: 9/10. Date read: 2023-11-15. Best travel book I’ve ever read! Shook my soul many times. Tiny “daily meditation” format, with lots of quotes from others, but wow what wonderful insights. They make me yearn to travel again. Love love love these ideas and perspectives so much.

title: Finite and Infinite Games
author: James P. Carse
context: Finite and Infinite Games - by James P. Carse Recommend it: 9/10. Date read: 2023-10-10. So abstract. Maybe the most abstract book you’ll ever read. Compares “finite” games with rules and winners, versus “infinite” games without winners where we can play with the game itself. Is it about a job versus a calling? Religion versus spirituality? A story versus story-telling? Who knows. Thought-provoking if you can apply the metaphor to whatever concerns you.

title: How Minds Change
author: David McRaney
context: How Minds Change - by David McRaney Recommend it: 9/10. Date read: 2023-07-30. The psychology of how and why we believe. How we learn and change. The craft of doubt and persuasion. Insights into the social definition of truth. Epistemology. Certainty is a feeling not based on facts. Well-written with a nice balance of story-telling and deeper dives.

title: How Religion Evolved
author: Robin Dunbar
context: How Religion Evolved - by Robin Dunbar Recommend it: 9/10. Date read: 2023-07-20. Great anthropology! So many insights into religions, tribes, friendships, organizations, the evolution of minds, superstition, and more. Got me thinking most about friendships.

title: Nothing & Everything
author: Val N. Tine
context: Nothing & Everything - by Val N. Tine Recommend it: 9/10. Date read: 2023-06-22. I love this book so much. It's the joy of nihilism. Nothing is true. Everything is permitted. I agree completely. I would give it a 10-out-of-10 rating but I disliked the whole second half of the book. So just read the first half. See my notes here. If you like my book “Useful Not True”, you should read this.

title: You Look Like a Thing and I Love You
author: Janelle Shane
context: You Look Like a Thing and I Love You - by Janelle Shane Recommend it: 9/10. Date read: 2023-06-18. A funny book explaining the basics of AI! The subtitle is How Artificial Intelligence Works and Why It's Making the World a Weirder Place. A great introduction to AI. With a cute cartoon mascot. The title is from her training an AI to write romantic greeting cards.

title: City of Gold: Dubai
author: Jim Krane
context: City of Gold: Dubai - by Jim Krane Recommend it: 9/10. Date read: 2023-06-17. So well-written! Absolutely fascinating history of Dubai. An exciting page-turner. It gave me so much admiration for the city and its visionaries.

title: The Righteous Mind
author: Jonathan Haidt
context: The Righteous Mind - by Jonathan Haidt Recommend it: 9/10. Date read: 2023-05-28. Brilliant insights into human nature. Moral reasoning, inventing victims, emotional reactions, the elephant (emotions) and its rider (explanations). Intuition reacts then logic confabulates a reason. Survival of the fittest applied to groups. Understanding religion and tradition. Great from start to finish.

title: Write Useful Books
author: Rob Fitzpatrick
context: Write Useful Books - by Rob Fitzpatrick Recommend it: 9/10. Date read: 2022-09-25. How to write a non-fiction book so useful to people that they recommend it to others. A great step-by-step methodology from someone experienced, who’s done it successfully a few times already.

title: Wild Problems
author: Russ Roberts
context: Wild Problems - by Russ Roberts Recommend it: 9/10. Date read: 2022-09-12. How to improve your HUGE major life decisions, like whether/who to marry, whether to have kids, where to live, career paths, and such — where you can’t use the usual checklist/data approach. This economist addresses self-identity, “deepest self”, and “something I was meant to do”. You can’t use a pro/con checklist with an item that says “lose respect for myself”.

title: Relationship Handbook
author: George Pransky
context: Relationship Handbook - by George Pransky Recommend it: 9/10. Date read: 2022-08-16. Best philosophy of love relationships I’ve ever found. Like meditation teaches you that moods pass, this experienced marriage counselor says this applies to relationship communication as well. When angry or insecure, don’t vent, don’t share that. Let the feeling pass. Your anger doesn’t reveal some real truth. Everyone in a romantic relationship should read this.

title: Awaken the Giant Within
author: Tony Robbins
context: Awaken the Giant Within - by Tony Robbins Recommend it: 9/10. Date read: 2022-06-22. This 1992 book changed everything about my life. It’s my Bible. Most of my beliefs come from it. I read it many times at a formative age, but re-read it now 30 years later, taking notes. It’s not a perfect book. It’s too verbose and full of expired American references. But its core messages are the wisest, most effective life philosophy I’ve ever encountered. You choose how you feel. Your emotions come from you, not events or others. Doesn’t matter what’s true, but what empowers you. You adopted beliefs randomly from circumstance, but you can rewire your mind to believe whatever helps you be who you want to be. You have absolute control over your internal world. If you think, “I can’t help the way I feel”, you need this book.

title: How Buildings Learn
author: Stewart Brand
context: How Buildings Learn - by Stewart Brand Recommend it: 9/10. Date read: 2021-08-02. I’ve read this book three times since 1999, and gifted it many times to others. It’s changed the way I look at buildings. I read it again now because I’m building a new house. Its main idea is that all buildings are predictions, and all predictions are wrong, so design to make them easy to change. I think of it metaphorically in life: assuming my predictions about what I want will probably be wrong, so make my life easy to change. Get the paper book because the photos are crucial.

title: Getting Things Done
author: David Allen
context: Getting Things Done - by David Allen Recommend it: 9/10. Date read: 2021-04-30. Classic book with near-cult following. How to manage every last itty bitty tiny thing in your life. Keep your inbox empty. Re-read 16 years later. Still great.

title: Several Short Sentences About Writing
author: Verlyn Klinkenborg
context: Several Short Sentences About Writing - by Verlyn Klinkenborg Recommend it: 9/10. Date read: 2021-03-28. The 2nd-best and most-radical book about great writing. It tells you to focus entirely on the sentence, an approach that was already my favorite, which is why I bought this book. It recommends you boldly eliminate transitions and conjunctions, split compound sentences, don't save your point for the end, and revise by deleting. This is the first book I've seen printed as one sentence per line — a way I've been writing for many years, and now printed in my book “How to Live”.

title: Skin in the Game
author: Nassim Nicholas Taleb
context: Skin in the Game - by Nassim Nicholas Taleb Recommend it: 9/10. Date read: 2020-08-15. Taleb is always filled with surprising ideas and confrontational bragging. Ignore the hot air and gather the gems. Great thoughts around putting your ass on the line with consequences — not just thinking things in theory but doing things in reality — in the real world.

title: This Is Marketing
author: Seth Godin
context: This Is Marketing - by Seth Godin Recommend it: 9/10. Date read: 2019-08-02. A must-read for every entrepreneur. A holistic, generous, human, emotional, long-term, story-driven approach to your business. The world would be a much better place if businesses were led this way. You'll have a competitive advantage if you do this, since so few do.

title: Atomic Habits
author: James Clear
context: Atomic Habits - by James Clear Recommend it: 9/10. Date read: 2018-12-29. I was doubtful, but everyone kept telling me it’s awesome, so I reluctantly read it. Holy crap! It’s GREAT! Feels like the definitive masterpiece on the subject of how to make good habits and break bad ones. Very focused on helping you take action. Very relatable and inspiring.

title: Thinking in Bets
author: Annie Duke
context: Thinking in Bets - by Annie Duke Recommend it: 9/10. Date read: 2018-06-02. Amazing point: Would your belief in something stand up to the question, “Wanna bet?” If you had to gamble significant money on that belief, would you still feel 100% about it? Or maybe more honestly 60%? This creates healthy skepticism encouraging you to seek the best information instead of just defending your belief. Now objective accuracy wins instead of argument. Combine with “The Biggest Bluff” by Maria Konnikova

title: 12 Rules for Life
author: Jordan Peterson
context: 12 Rules for Life - by Jordan Peterson Recommend it: 9/10. Date read: 2018-04-10. A unique thinker with strong opinions presented as indisputable fact. More surprisingly interesting ideas than almost any book I've ever read. Extremely thoughtful, but occasionally abruptly concludes with an unsupported point. It has a conservative “this is how it is” certainty. It’s a broad collection of thoughtful insights on life, mixed with a lot of Bible interpretation.

title: Sapiens
author: Yuval Noah Harari
context: Sapiens - by Yuval Noah Harari Recommend it: 9/10. Date read: 2017-08-15. I resisted reading this popular history of mankind, because it came out when I had just finished “Guns, Germs, and Steel” and “Cows, Pigs, Wars, and Witches”, on the same subject. But wow - this book is at its best when the author is sharing his personal perspective about binding myths, humanism, and other ways that “truths” are not true. And you get an interesting history of the world along with it. Strange mix of history and philosophy.

title: Happy
author: Derren Brown
context: Happy - by Derren Brown Recommend it: 9/10. Date read: 2017-03-05. Brilliant and profound yet totally entertaining philosophy book by one of my favorite people. Gives an approachable overview of past philosophies and shows how they apply to your life today better than the harmful pop-self-help-positivity stuff. Amazing perspectives on desires, death, relationships, anger, and how being present doesn’t matter as much as the story you tell yourself afterwards. His fun writing style isn’t reflected in my notes here. Get the book.

title: Au Contraire: Figuring Out the French
author: Gilles Asselin and Ruth Mastron
context: Au Contraire: Figuring Out the French - by Gilles Asselin and Ruth Mastron Recommend it: 9/10. Date read: 2016-10-11. The absolute best book I've ever found on explaining the mindset of a country. (Runner-up is “Watching the English” by Kate Fox.) I wish every country had a book this deep. Not just what but why! Also appreciate the bold writing, skipping caveats.

title: The Subtle Art of Not Giving a Fuck
author: Mark Manson
context: The Subtle Art of Not Giving a Fuck - by Mark Manson Recommend it: 9/10. Date read: 2016-09-26. The opposite of every other book. Don’t try. Give up. Be wrong. Lower your standards. Stop believing in yourself. Follow the pain. And oh yeah, kill yourself. Each point is profoundly true, useful, and more powerful than the usual positivity. Succinct but surprisingly deep, I read it in one night, then read it again a month later.

title: Ego Is the Enemy
author: Ryan Holiday
context: Ego Is the Enemy - by Ryan Holiday Recommend it: 9/10. Date read: 2016-08-01. Forget yourself and focus on the work. Be humble and persistent. Value discipline and results, not passion and confidence. Be lesser, do more. This message is crucial, but the opposite of almost every other book. I wish everyone would read this. I need to re-read it each year. It's that important. It's easy to read this and say “oh yeah I've got my ego under control”, but the problem is deeper than that.

title: Too Soon Old, Too Late Smart
author: Gordon Livingston
context: Too Soon Old, Too Late Smart - by Gordon Livingston Recommend it: 9/10. Date read: 2016-04-26. Powerful and profound life lessons from a psychiatrist who's been listening to people's problems for decades.

title: Cows, Pigs, Wars, and Witches
author: Marvin Harris
context: Cows, Pigs, Wars, and Witches - by Marvin Harris Recommend it: 9/10. Date read: 2016-02-19. Mind-blowing anthropology. Great argument that the reasons that religions worship cows or hate pigs, that tribes wage wars, or Europe's 200 years of witch hunts, are all very practical economic reasons usually unknown to the participants or washed out of history. But they're revealed here in zoomed-out hindsight. My notes here can't describe it. You have to read the whole book. Riveting.

title: The Entrepreneur Roller Coaster
author: Darren Hardy
context: The Entrepreneur Roller Coaster - by Darren Hardy Recommend it: 9/10. Date read: 2015-08-01. Rar! My heart rate is racing as I tear through this riveting book. Darren captures and spreads the entrepreneurial spirit better than anyone I know. I've been a successful entrepreneur for 25 years but The Entrepreneur Roller Coaster just got me more excited and enlightened than I've been in a long time. You must read and USE this immediately!

title: The Wisdom of No Escape
author: Pema Chödrön
context: The Wisdom of No Escape - by Pema Chödrön Recommend it: 9/10. Date read: 2015-04-16. Powerful thoughts on not running, distracting, or escaping, but sticking with something all the way through.

title: When Things Fall Apart
author: Pema Chödrön
context: When Things Fall Apart - by Pema Chödrön Recommend it: 9/10. Date read: 2014-11-30. Profound philosophy on facing the negative emotions head-on and getting to know them well, instead of trying to avoid them or escape.

title: The Compound Effect
author: Darren Hardy
context: The Compound Effect - by Darren Hardy Recommend it: 9/10. Date read: 2014-07-17. Classic self-help book, in the best sense. Inspired the hell out of me. Mostly fundamentals I had heard before, but put in a very energetic go-do-it way. As he says, “You already know all that you need to succeed. You don’t need to learn anything more. If all we needed was more information, everyone with an Internet connection would live in a mansion, have abs of steel, and be blissfully happy.”

title: When Cultures Collide
author: Richard D. Lewis
context: When Cultures Collide - by Richard D. Lewis Recommend it: 9/10. Date read: 2014-07-16. Masterpiece of cultural observations. I wish there were more books like this. My Wood Egg books were created with the same goal. Insights into different countries' cultures. Some amazing, like the reason for American's lack of manners, or Japanese procedures. My detailed notes don't do it justice because I practically underlined the entire book, I loved it so much.

title: Antifragile
author: Nassim Nicholas Taleb
context: Antifragile - by Nassim Nicholas Taleb Recommend it: 9/10. Date read: 2013-05-15. Bold perspectives, unusual ideas, and surprisingly wise advice around an interesting subject of the “opposite of fragile.” Looking through that lens at health, education, governments, business, and life philosophy. Very inspiring, and sparks a lot of further discussion.

title: The Willpower Instinct
author: Kelly McGonigal
context: The Willpower Instinct - by Kelly McGonigal Recommend it: 9/10. Date read: 2013-02-05. Amazing book about willpower from Stanford psychology professor who teaches just this. Killer first point: The best way to improve your self-control is to see how and why you lose control. This is a better book than the other book on Willpower here on my list, because it's more actionable, better written, better presented. Really amazing (IF you act on it!)

title: Turning Pro
author: Steven Pressfield
context: Turning Pro - by Steven Pressfield Recommend it: 9/10. Date read: 2012-10-25. In the same vein as his other books “Do the Work” and ”War of Art” - but a message that needs to be said again and again to really get through. It's all about the resistance, avoiding distractions, getting serious. Here he dives more into the mindset shift of thinking of your art as a hobby versus a real career. This stuff shakes me to the core, every time.

title: Quiet
author: Susan Cain
context: Quiet - by Susan Cain Recommend it: 9/10. Date read: 2012-09-22. Any introvert should like this book. Wonderful info and insights about introversion. It'll help you defend your preference for low-stimulus environments. Since reading it, I feel better about insisting on my quiet/alone time.

title: Brain Rules for Baby
author: John Medina
context: Brain Rules for Baby - by John Medina Recommend it: 9/10. Date read: 2011-11-11. My single favorite baby book: written by a neuroscientist, about babies’ brain development from pregnancy to children. Single best book for soon-to-be parents to read. I didn’t want kids until I read it, then it actually got me excited about the process. I’ve recommended it more than a hundred times.

title: Do the Work
author: Steven Pressfield
context: Do the Work - by Steven Pressfield Recommend it: 9/10. Date read: 2011-10-25. A true manifesto. A call to action. A kick in the butt for any creative person. Great thoughts on overcoming the resistance to creating.

title: What Got You Here Won’t Get You There
author: Marshall Goldsmith
context: What Got You Here Won’t Get You There - by Marshall Goldsmith Recommend it: 9/10. Date read: 2011-08-22. Aimed at already-successful people. The personality traits that brought you to success (personal discipline, saying yes to everything, over-confidence) are the same traits that hold you back from going further! (Where you need to listen to lead, and don't let over-confidence make you over-commit.) Stinging counter-intuitive insights that hit very close to home for me. Great specific suggestions for how to improve.

title: A Guide to the Good Life: The Ancient Art of Stoic Joy
author: William Irvine
context: A Guide to the Good Life: The Ancient Art of Stoic Joy - by William Irvine Recommend it: 9/10. Date read: 2010-09-26. Almost too personal for me to give an objective review, because I found when reading it that the quirky philosophy I've been living my life by since 17 matches up exactly with a 2000-year-old philosophy called Stoicism. Mine was self-developed haphazardly, so it was fascinating to read the refined developed original. Really resonated.

title: Switch
author: Chip Heath and Dan Heath
context: Switch - by Chip Heath and Dan Heath Recommend it: 9/10. Date read: 2010-05-10. Great great great great GREAT psychology book about real ways to make change last - both personal and organizational. So many powerful insights, based on fact not theory. Inspiring counterintuitive stories of huge organizational change against all odds. Highly recommended for everyone.

title: The Happiness Hypothesis
author: Jonathan Haidt
context: The Happiness Hypothesis - by Jonathan Haidt Recommend it: 9/10. Date read: 2010-05-01. Psychology professor's digestible but deep insight into how our minds work, around the topic of happiness. Great metaphor of a rider on the back of an elephant. Rider is reasoning, elephant is emotions. Rider has limited control of what the elephant does. Surprising insights into ethics and morality. See my notes for great quotes, but read the whole well-written book.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
context: Influence - by Robert Cialdini Recommend it: 9/10. Date read: 2009-08-15. Classic book on the psychology of persuasion. I read it 15 years ago, thought about it ever since, and re-read it now. How to get a 700% improvement in volunteers. How to sell more by doubling your prices. How to make people feel they made a choice, when really you made it for them.

title: The Time Paradox
author: Philip Zimbardo and John Boyd
context: The Time Paradox - by Philip Zimbardo and John Boyd Recommend it: 9/10. Date read: 2009-04-03. Profound idea that everyone has a primary time focus, either Future-focused, Present-focused, or Past-focused. Fascinating implications of each. Because I’m so future-focused, reading this book helped me understand people who are very present-focused. Also great advice on shifting your focus when needed. I read it 14 years ago, but still think about it constantly.

title: How to Get Rich
author: Felix Dennis
context: How to Get Rich - by Felix Dennis Recommend it: 9/10. Date read: 2008-06-18. Shockingly honest thoughts from a filthy rich bastard.

title: The 4-Hour Work Week
author: Tim Ferriss
context: The 4-Hour Work Week - by Tim Ferriss Recommend it: 9/10. Date read: 2008-05-15. Brilliant reversal of all of the “how to manage all your crap” books. This one tells you how to say “no” to the crap, set expectations on your terms, and be just as effective in a fraction of the time.

title: The Smartest Investment Book You’ll Ever Read
author: Daniel R. Solin
context: The Smartest Investment Book You’ll Ever Read - by Daniel R. Solin Recommend it: 9/10. Date read: 2008-05-14. An itty-bitty quick-read no-fluff book with the wisest succinct advice to investors: You can't predict the future, and neither can anyone else. Determine your asset allocation, stick with cheap broad indexes, and rebalance occasionally.

title: The Paradox of Choice - Why More is Less
author: Barry Schwartz
context: The Paradox of Choice - Why More is Less - by Barry Schwartz Recommend it: 9/10. Date read: 2007-07-11. Faced with many options or decisions in your life? This will change the way you look at them. We feel worse when we have too many options.

title: The Art of Profitability
author: Adrian Slywotzky
context: The Art of Profitability - by Adrian Slywotzky Recommend it: 9/10. Date read: 2005-12-02. 25 different models of profitability presented in examples you can relate to your own business, making you realize profit-sources you’d never thought of before.

title: Private Revolutions
author: Yuan Yang
context: Private Revolutions - by Yuan Yang Recommend it: 8/10. Date read: 2026-06-15. Non-fiction story of four real women in current China, following their lives from childhood in the 1990s until 2023 when the book was published. I love her direct writing style, and the stories were pretty fascinating. A great 3rd or 4th book to help understand contemporary Chinese culture.

title: Tribal
author: Michael Morris
context: Tribal - by Michael Morris Recommend it: 8/10. Date read: 2026-04-16. I love cultural psychology. Great insights here, and examples of how change happens, on the personal level, cultural level, and even institutional level. American, but lived in Hong Kong for years and I appreciated his example of Singapore.

title: Elephant in the Brain
author: Kevin Simler and Robin Hanson
context: Elephant in the Brain - by Kevin Simler and Robin Hanson Recommend it: 8/10. Date read: 2026-03-30. You have hidden motives and subconscious incentives. Two reasons for doing anything: a good reason and the real reason. Instititutions do this too: wasteful because they’re serving hidden purposes no one acknowledges. Great insights throughout.

title: Argumentative Indian
author: Amartya Sen
context: Argumentative Indian - by Amartya Sen Recommend it: 8/10. Date read: 2025-12-25. Famous analysis of India’s intellectual and political heritage, quite against Hindu nationalism. I learned a lot. I’d happily read ten more books like this.

title: Factfulness
author: Hans Rosling
context: Factfulness - by Hans Rosling Recommend it: 8/10. Date read: 2025-12-12. What a great man. Empathy and charity embodied. I love his worldview. Written as he was dying. Its main message is to help us see the world more accurately - to see how much it’s improved. Shows why we tend towards us-versus-them stories, the difference between frightening versus dangerous, focusing on the system.

title: Charisma Myth
author: Olivia Fox Cabane
context: Charisma Myth - by Olivia Fox Cabane Recommend it: 8/10. Date read: 2025-12-01. Your body language, mannerisms, speaking habits, listening habits, all affect how you’re perceived. Many tips in here sound manipulative (to convey power, take up more space) - but are ultimately about helping your outside match your inside, for the desired effect including helping people feel more comfortable around you, more seen and understood. Empathetic advice like making sure you’re sitting at a 90° angle instead of directly across from someone, and making sure their back is not to an open space with people moving behind them, which makes us feel uncomfortable. I use these tips when meeting with strangers.

title: How to Know a Person
author: David Brooks
context: How to Know a Person - by David Brooks Recommend it: 8/10. Date read: 2025-11-26. First part was great - so empathetic - about how and why to really get to know someone. I skipped the middle part about difficult conversations in the Culture Wars. Last part was great, about what it is to be wise.

title: Mathematica
author: David Bessis, Kevin Frey
context: Mathematica - by David Bessis, Kevin Frey Recommend it: 8/10. Date read: 2025-11-14. Math is imagination, visualization, and intuition. The symbols are just a language to explain the mind’s image - like sheet music. You can train your intuition and develop visualization skills with practice. Math is an inner tool to enhance human cognition, more akin to psychology.

title: Advice on Upskilling
author: Justin Skycak
context: Advice on Upskilling - by Justin Skycak Recommend it: 8/10. Date read: 2025-10-09. Super motivating book about effective learning and improvement. He’s a math, memory, and weightlifting expert from justinmath.com and MathAcademy.com, so the advice leans that way a bit, but applies to anything you want to learn.

title: Fossil Future
author: Alex Epstein
context: Fossil Future - by Alex Epstein Recommend it: 8/10. Date read: 2025-07-04. Fascinating. I highly recommend this if you want to practice changing a long-held belief. It argues that because fossil fuels are still the most cost-effective energy, essential for human flourishing, and billions of people are suffering for lack of cost-effective energy, we should not discourage their use. While I don’t care much about this specific subject, I loved learning about the knowledge system that takes (1) raw research, (2) summarizes it, (3) disseminates it to the public and decision-makers, and (4) evaluates what actions we should take — but each of steps 2-3-4 can distort the expert knowledge from step 1.

title: Don’t Be a Feminist
author: Bryan Caplan
context: Don’t Be a Feminist - by Bryan Caplan Recommend it: 8/10. Date read: 2025-06-30. Don’t let the title distract you. This is not a book about feminism but a brilliant philosophy book about genuine justice. A collection of simple applicable essays applying logic, economics, and empathy to every-day situations. Clear and surprising thoughts.

title: This Is Strategy
author: Seth Godin
context: This Is Strategy - by Seth Godin Recommend it: 8/10. Date read: 2024-06-13. Classic Seth Godin at his best. Hopefully you know what I mean. Hundreds of individual insights that comprise a worldview worth adopting.

title: Philosophy of Software Design
author: John K. Ousterhout
context: Philosophy of Software Design - by John K. Ousterhout Recommend it: 8/10. Date read: 2024-06-10. Programming wisdom: modular design, keep APIs simple, how to avoid complexity, etc. Great insights from experience.

title: Dawn of Eurasia
author: Bruno Maçães
context: Dawn of Eurasia - by Bruno Maçães Recommend it: 8/10. Date read: 2024-04-23. Portuguese political thinker travels the border between Europe and Asia with the view that this border is moot. Great cultural insights and observations. I love this stuff.

title: Dreaming in Chinese
author: Deborah Fallows
context: Dreaming in Chinese - by Deborah Fallows Recommend it: 8/10. Date read: 2024-03-12. American lived in China for three years and wrote this adorable book about the Chinese language and some cultural insights. Instead of shopkeepers saying “have a nice day” they say “walk slowly”. The word for “careful” means “small heart”. Many more like this. 热闹 “hot noisy” helped explain something I had always wondered about Chinese culture.

title: The Silk Roads
author: Peter Frankopan
context: The Silk Roads - by Peter Frankopan Recommend it: 8/10. Date read: 2023-10-18. A children’s illustrated book that I started reading to my boy, but enjoyed it more myself. I’m so curious about the subject, but was glad to have the succinct entertaining version, which was just enough. Taught me so much history I’d never heard before.

title: The Religious Case Against Belief
author: James P. Carse
context: The Religious Case Against Belief - by James P. Carse Recommend it: 8/10. Date read: 2023-10-15. Theology surprise, differentiating belief and religion, belief and faith. So many unique insights. So interesting to hear a theologian’s stance against believers, in favor of “higher ignorance”.

title: Pragmatism
author: William James
context: Pragmatism - by William James Recommend it: 8/10. Date read: 2022-12-24. Transcript of lectures given at Harvard about the philosophy of Pragmatism. I especially liked his thoughts on pluralism vs monism. This made me want to read more of his writing. The 1800’s speaking style takes a bit of effort to parse.

title: Complete Idiot’s Guide to Understanding Judaism
author: Rabbi Benjamin Blech
context: Complete Idiot’s Guide to Understanding Judaism - by Rabbi Benjamin Blech Recommend it: 8/10. Date read: 2022-12-14. Really interesting and entertainingly written. I didn't realize what a complete system Judaism is, dictating almost every decision in life.

title: Code
author: Charles Petzold
context: Code - by Charles Petzold Recommend it: 8/10. Date read: 2022-09-24. Masterpiece of clear explanation! How to make a computer from scratch. Basics of electricity, 1/0 AND/OR switches, boolean algebra, how physical switches can make an adding machine, bytes and ASCII text, memory, CPU, and so on, up to a working computer. Each chapter building perfectly on the previous. If you’re interested in learning computers from scratch, this is the definitive book for it. (I rate this book a perfect 10 for what it is, but only giving an 8 here, because it’s not for everyone.)

title: The Biggest Bluff
author: Maria Konnikova
context: The Biggest Bluff - by Maria Konnikova Recommend it: 8/10. Date read: 2022-09-10. Amazing use of poker to form a philosophy of probability, intuition, instant karma, taming your emotions, treating triumph and disaster the same, and agency. Brilliant writing, mixing real-life events with philosophical pauses. Rare mix of riveting and thoughtful. Combine with “Thinking in Bets” by Annie Duke.

title: The Secrets of Story
author: Matt Bird
context: The Secrets of Story - by Matt Bird Recommend it: 8/10. Date read: 2022-08-02. Amazing insights into what makes great stories work, and bad ones fail. Emphasizes the importance of irony: the meaningful gap between expectation and reality. Specifically about screenwriting for film/tv, but fascinating even if you never plan to write a screenplay. Gives you deeper appreciation of the movies you’ve loved. And along the way, some good insights about life itself.

title: Philosophy: a Complete Introduction
author: Sharon Kaye
context: Philosophy: a Complete Introduction - by Sharon Kaye Recommend it: 8/10. Date read: 2022-07-26. Very thought-provoking overview of philosophers like Plato, Aristotle, Hume, Descartes, Kant, Nietzsche, Sartre. But the author does an AMAZING job of making everything incredibly clear, understandable, relateable, and applicable. So well-written. I’ve read a few books in this genre, but this is the best by far. I highly recommend this to anyone.

title: The Minimalist Entrepreneur
author: Sahil Lavingia
context: The Minimalist Entrepreneur - by Sahil Lavingia Recommend it: 8/10. Date read: 2022-04-30. A must-read for any potential founder of a small online business. Brilliant insights into starting something simply and sensibly. Best guide to the new world of starting from anywhere.

title: Four Thousand Weeks
author: Oliver Burkeman
context: Four Thousand Weeks - by Oliver Burkeman Recommend it: 8/10. Date read: 2022-02-21. Give up hope and embrace your limits. Everything you do means giving up something else. Say yes to less. He’s one of my favorite authors, so wonderfully thorough, but I already agree and am living this way. (My “Hell Yeah or No” was about this subject.) Still, I’d recommend it to anyone.

title: How to Live on 24 Hours a Day
author: Arnold Bennett
context: How to Live on 24 Hours a Day - by Arnold Bennett Recommend it: 8/10. Date read: 2022-01-25. Delightful quick droll funny old book from 1908 about how to make the best use of your time. I like his written voice. I like his points on poetry, novels, curiosity, empathy, martyrs, reading the news, and of course making the most of every minute you have.

title: How to Think More Effectively
author: the School of Life
context: How to Think More Effectively - by the School of Life Recommend it: 8/10. Date read: 2022-01-21. Great little book by Alain de Botton with quick pop-philosophy and life advice. Surprisingly good insights on how to be a better friend and listener, using envy, writing like Proust, and the companionship of book subjects.

title: Story
author: Robert McKee
context: Story - by Robert McKee Recommend it: 8/10. Date read: 2021-12-26. A masterpiece about screenwriting. Everyone who writes fiction must read this book. Cinema fans should read this book, even if you have no intention to write. It’s a film school masterclass. It also has surprisingly good insights into life: the story we all create by living.

title: All I Really Need to Know I Learned in Kindergarten
author: Robert Fulghum
context: All I Really Need to Know I Learned in Kindergarten - by Robert Fulghum Recommend it: 8/10. Date read: 2021-10-31. I read and loved these stories 30 years ago, so read again for tips on story-telling. I admire his way of taking tiny concrete every-day things or situations, and relating them to life-size big-picture humanity themes.

title: Nonviolent Communication
author: Marshall Rosenberg
context: Nonviolent Communication - by Marshall Rosenberg Recommend it: 8/10. Date read: 2021-10-20. After years of so many people telling how much this book has helped them, I finally read it. And yeah, it’s impressive. Very compassionate and actively empathetic. Everyone who communicates should read this and take it to heart.

title: Open Borders
author: Bryan Caplan
context: Open Borders - by Bryan Caplan Recommend it: 8/10. Date read: 2021-08-30. A nonfiction comic book, by an economist, about unrestricted immigration. What? Yeah. Everyone should read it. This fun easy read of a single well-argued point will change your mind no matter what your previous stance. Brilliant illustration by Zach Weinersmith helps make the topic stick. NOTE: Don’t try to read it on a little black-and-white Kindle. It really is a comic book and needs to be read full-size in color.

title: The Practice
author: Seth Godin
context: The Practice - by Seth Godin Recommend it: 8/10. Date read: 2021-01-15. The subtitle “Shipping Creative Work” sums it up well. It’s a great call-to-action, giving you the right mindset to create the thing you know you need to do. Very encouraging and motivating. Every creative person needs this.

title: The Psychology of Money
author: Morgan Housel
context: The Psychology of Money - by Morgan Housel Recommend it: 8/10. Date read: 2020-10-01. Thoughts on wealth, greed, and happiness. Good insights into the investing mindset. Well-written without fluff. Some great counter-intuitive surprises.

title: No More Mr. Nice Guy
author: Robert Glover
context: No More Mr. Nice Guy - by Robert Glover Recommend it: 8/10. Date read: 2020-07-10. Nice guys need to read this book about love and sex.

title: Stillness Is the Key
author: Ryan Holiday
context: Stillness Is the Key - by Ryan Holiday Recommend it: 8/10. Date read: 2020-06-25. Peaceful thoughts on inner tranquility and focus. Great writer, solid ideas, I love this. Read my notes for an idea, but definitely read the whole book.

title: Everything Is Fucked
author: Mark Manson
context: Everything Is Fucked - by Mark Manson Recommend it: 8/10. Date read: 2019-07-27. Philosophy made relatable. Great points about taking feelings seriously, pain as the speed of light, humanity as an ends not means, and democracy acknowledging human nature. Sections on Nietzsche and Kant are fascinating, not academic. The second half grabbed me the most.

title: Stubborn Attachments
author: Tyler Cowen
context: Stubborn Attachments - by Tyler Cowen Recommend it: 8/10. Date read: 2019-04-15. Subtitle “A Vision for a Society of Free, Prosperous, and Responsible Individuals” gives a hint of its contents. I love these kinds of books: full of well-considered, smart, rational and surprising ideas from an economist.

title: Watching the English
author: Kate Fox
context: Watching the English - by Kate Fox Recommend it: 8/10. Date read: 2018-10-01. The first book I read about a country’s philosophy, and still one of the best. (Au Contraire, about the French, is the other.) I re-read it now 11 years later, and loved her insights and writing. Active anthropology. A must-read if you’re spending time in England.

title: Story of Philosophy
author: Will Durant
context: Story of Philosophy - by Will Durant Recommend it: 8/10. Date read: 2018-07-20. Profiles of some top philosophers: Plato, Aristotle, Bacon, Voltaire, Kant, Schopenhauer, Nietzsche. But wow - Durant’s writing steals the show. A hundred various thoughts to digest.

title: Innumeracy
author: John Allen Paulos
context: Innumeracy - by John Allen Paulos Recommend it: 8/10. Date read: 2017-10-09. Why are so many people so mathematically illiterate? (Hence the title: illiteracy → innumeracy.) I wish I was an expert at this. I love it when someone is able to blow apart a claim in a minute, or know a good versus bad deal, just by running the numbers. I’d love to get great at this, then re-learn almost everything in life, but now with this additional lens.

title: The Dip
author: Seth Godin
context: The Dip - by Seth Godin Recommend it: 8/10. Date read: 2017-03-15. Tiny quick read with a punchy point: Anything worth doing has a painfully-hard middle period, which is where most people quit. But knowing this in advance, ask yourself seriously if you really have the dedication to stick it through that hard time. If not, then don’t begin! Quit in advance! But if so, then expect that dark dip, and don’t quit when you’re in it. Read the whole book if this applies to you. There’s not a wasted page.

title: The Road Less Traveled
author: M. Scott Peck
context: The Road Less Traveled - by M. Scott Peck Recommend it: 8/10. Date read: 2016-10-26. Profound truths and bold opinions on discipline, life, and love, written by a psychiatrist in 1978. It's been a best-seller all these years for a good reason.

title: Guns, Germs, and Steel
author: Jared Diamond
context: Guns, Germs, and Steel - by Jared Diamond Recommend it: 8/10. Date read: 2016-07-25. Why did the people of certain continents succeeded in invading other continents and conquering or displacing their people? Fascinating world history. Winner of the Pulitzer Prize. See the notes.

title: Steal Like an Artist
author: Austin Kleon
context: Steal Like an Artist - by Austin Kleon Recommend it: 8/10. Date read: 2016-05-10. Short, inspiring insights into creativity and the creative life: the day job, the mindset, etc. Also read his other book “Show Your Work”.

title: Total Recall
author: Arnold Schwarzenegger
context: Total Recall - by Arnold Schwarzenegger Recommend it: 8/10. Date read: 2016-05-05. I was not expecting to love this so much! I'm not a fan of his, but MAN his ambitious mindset, especially in his early days when he first moved to America, is so inspiring. Both on the movie-star side and real-estate side. If you need a role model or inspiration for thinking big, this is it. (Skip the final section on his governor days.) I was telling friends stories and thoughts about this book for weeks afterwards.

title: A Mind for Numbers
author: Barbara Oakley
context: A Mind for Numbers - by Barbara Oakley Recommend it: 8/10. Date read: 2015-03-03. Thought I was getting a book about math, but ended up being a surprisingly good book about learning in general. Main points are about diffused thinking vs focused thinking.

title: Smartcuts
author: Shane Snow
context: Smartcuts - by Shane Snow Recommend it: 8/10. Date read: 2014-11-20. Inspiring study of how successful people took smart shortcuts and bypassed the long-slogging dues-paying process. Great insights on momentum. Read the whole book for specific stories of Jimmy Fallon, Skrillex, Elon Musk, David Heinemeier Hansson, and Michelle Phan.

title: Superhuman by Habit
author: Tynan
context: Superhuman by Habit - by Tynan Recommend it: 8/10. Date read: 2014-10-10. Great little manifesto about habits. Very well thought-through practical applications, tips, and philosophies on creating and sustaining the habits you want.

title: Mindwise
author: Nicholas Epley
context: Mindwise - by Nicholas Epley Recommend it: 8/10. Date read: 2014-10-01. Many brilliant insights, especially about over-estimating the differences between you and others, thereby separating into us-vs-them tribalism.

title: The Obstacle Is the Way
author: Ryan Holiday
context: The Obstacle Is the Way - by Ryan Holiday Recommend it: 8/10. Date read: 2014-06-30. A succinct adrenaline-generating call to clear thinking and rational action. Many historical examples. Incredibly inspiring.

title: The Antidote
author: Oliver Burkeman
context: The Antidote - by Oliver Burkeman Recommend it: 8/10. Date read: 2014-06-28. Surprisingly deep and philosophical. The first book I've read in years that makes me want to read it twice. The title and cover make it seem like light pop, but it's a wonderfully-cynical British journalist diving into Stoicism, meditation, death, etc.

title: Decisive
author: Chip and Dan Heath
context: Decisive - by Chip and Dan Heath Recommend it: 8/10. Date read: 2014-06-27. Interesting and insightful dive into the subject of how to make big decisions. Specific useful advice.

title: 5 Elements of Effective Thinking
author: Edward B. Burger and Michael Starbird
context: 5 Elements of Effective Thinking - by Edward B. Burger and Michael Starbird Recommend it: 8/10. Date read: 2013-08-30. Short and brilliant book with tips on being a better thinker. Being persistent, thorough, rooted in fundamentals, creative, and a more active learner. Surprisingly inspiring.

title: The Icarus Deception
author: Seth Godin
context: The Icarus Deception - by Seth Godin Recommend it: 8/10. Date read: 2013-01-11. VERY interesting. Seth is moving from talking about business to talking about being an artist in the broad sense of anyone who creates (and ships!) something daring and new. I loved the distinction between the industrialist and the artist, as it helped me give a term for something I'd experienced: not being able to relate at all to those who just want to grow business for business' sake, whereas I always saw my business like a creative art project. The book stays very high-level, so don't look for “TO-DO” type tips.

title: So Good They Can’t Ignore You
author: Cal Newport
context: So Good They Can’t Ignore You - by Cal Newport Recommend it: 8/10. Date read: 2012-10-07. Shockingly smart thoughts about your career. A must-read for anyone who is not loving their work, wanting to quit their job, and follow their passion, or not sure what to do next. I'm recommending this many times a week to people who email me with these kinds of questions. Best book I've ever read on the subject. See https://commoncog.com/blog/so-good-they-cant-ignore-you/ for a better summary.

title: Mastery
author: George Leonard
context: Mastery - by George Leonard Recommend it: 8/10. Date read: 2012-10-01. A description of the path to mastery in any field: to enjoy regular practice for its own sake, to push your capabilities but to accept the plateau, to surrender to the path and exercises your teacher gives you. Stay focused, not distracted like the dabbler, impatient like the obsessive, or complacent like the hacker.

title: The Little Book of Talent
author: Daniel Coyle
context: The Little Book of Talent - by Daniel Coyle Recommend it: 8/10. Date read: 2012-09-08. First he wrote The Talent Code, which I also highly recommend, then he distilled all that research about deliberate practice into 52 actionable tips. Amazing and inspiring, you can read the whole thing in 90 minutes, then get to work!

title: What Technology Wants
author: Kevin Kelly
context: What Technology Wants - by Kevin Kelly Recommend it: 8/10. Date read: 2012-04-26. Fascinating historical and philosophical perspective on technology, where it's come from, where it's going.

title: Thinking, Fast and Slow
author: Daniel Kahneman
context: Thinking, Fast and Slow - by Daniel Kahneman Recommend it: 8/10. Date read: 2011-12-08. If you liked “Predictably Irrational” or “Stumbling on Happiness” or any of those pop-psychology books, well, this is the Godfather of all of their work. Huge thorough book gives a great overview of much of his work. Read the other quotes on Amazon about it.

title: Willpower
author: Roy Baumeister and John Tierney
context: Willpower - by Roy Baumeister and John Tierney Recommend it: 8/10. Date read: 2011-09-09. You have a finite amount of willpower that becomes depleted as you use it. Two traits that consistently predict “positive outcomes” in life: intelligence and self-control. Most major problems, personal and social, center on failure of self-control. When people were asked about their failings, a lack of self-control was at the top of the list. So let's talk about self-control....

title: Power of Full Engagement
author: Jim Loehr and Tony Schwartz
context: Power of Full Engagement - by Jim Loehr and Tony Schwartz Recommend it: 8/10. Date read: 2011-09-03. The authors worked with the best athletes and executives for years, and found that the best ones knew how to push themselves, then recuperate, push, recuperate. Take this same approach to your emotional, mental, physical, and even spiritual life, and it's a powerful metaphor. Think of sprints, not marathons. Be fully in whatever you're in, then give time to recuperate. But push further each time, past your comfort zone, like a good exercise plan.

title: Moonwalking with Einstein
author: Joshua Foer
context: Moonwalking with Einstein - by Joshua Foer Recommend it: 8/10. Date read: 2011-06-18. For those fascinated with memory. Riveting page-turner about a journalist (with no particularly good memory) who went to cover a memory championship event. Intrigued and befriending some competitors, he starts practicing, and a year later wins the U.S. memory championship event himself. Inspiring dive into the subject of memorization.

title: Practicing Mind
author: Thomas Sterner
context: Practicing Mind - by Thomas Sterner Recommend it: 8/10. Date read: 2011-05-27. Great simple philosophy: Life itself is one long practice session. Everything in life worth achieving requires practice. Practice is not just for artistic or athletic skill, but practicing patience, practicing communication, practicing anything you do in life. The process/practice itself is the real goal, not the outcome.

title: The Personal MBA
author: Josh Kaufman
context: The Personal MBA - by Josh Kaufman Recommend it: 8/10. Date read: 2011-02-16. An amazing overview of everything you need to know about business. Covers all the basics, minus buzz-words and fluff. Look at my notes for an example, but read the whole book. One of the most inspiring things I've read in years. Want proof? I asked the author to be my coach/mentor afterwards. It's that good.

title: Mindset
author: Carol Dweck
context: Mindset - by Carol Dweck Recommend it: 8/10. Date read: 2010-11-27. Crucial distinction: People in a “fixed” mindset believe that you *are* great or flawed. People in a “growth” mindset believe your greatness (or flaws) are because of your actions. The fixed mindset is very harmful in every area of life (work, art, relationships, business, etc.) We get our initial mindset from our environment. When parents say, “You are great,” instead of ”You did great work,” they accidentally create the “fixed” mindset.

title: Art and Fear
author: David Bayles and Ted Orland
context: Art and Fear - by David Bayles and Ted Orland Recommend it: 8/10. Date read: 2010-11-23. For artists and musicians only: beautiful insights into the creative process.

title: Drive
author: Daniel Pink
context: Drive - by Daniel Pink Recommend it: 8/10. Date read: 2010-09-01. Essential for all managers. Deep surprising study of motivation at work. Extrinsic vs intrinsic. Work vs play. When money is used as an external reward for some activity, the subjects lose intrinsic interest for the activity.

title: The Geography of Bliss
author: Eric Weiner
context: The Geography of Bliss - by Eric Weiner Recommend it: 8/10. Date read: 2010-01-20. Cranky NPR reporter dives deep into Iceland, Bhutan, Qatar, Holland, Switzerland, Thailand, India and Moldova to find out why people are happy (or not) in each. So beautifully written with astounding insights into culture and happiness. Amazing. Been thinking about it for weeks afterwards.

title: How We Decide
author: Jonah Lehrer
context: How We Decide - by Jonah Lehrer Recommend it: 8/10. Date read: 2009-11-10. Brilliant book with one clear message: our emotional brain is faster and usually smarter than our logical brain. Our emotions are trained by years of logic and experience, retaining it all for real wisdom. Many decisions are better made by going with the gut feeling. Gets a little too technical with deep brain/neuro/cortex talk, but brings it back to usable points.

title: Discover Your Inner Economist
author: Tyler Cowen
context: Discover Your Inner Economist - by Tyler Cowen Recommend it: 8/10. Date read: 2009-10-19. Recommendations for the transactions of life. When to give to charity, what restaurants to choose, what insurance to buy, etc. He makes a rational case for these, often surprising, from an economics point of view.

title: The Talent Code
author: Daniel Coyle
context: The Talent Code - by Daniel Coyle Recommend it: 8/10. Date read: 2009-08-22. A great book showing that deep practice - (struggling in certain targeted ways - operating at the edges of your ability, where you make mistakes - experiences where you're forced to slow down, make errors, and correct them) - is what really makes you improve at anything.

title: Ignore Everybody
author: Hugh MacLeod
context: Ignore Everybody - by Hugh MacLeod Recommend it: 8/10. Date read: 2009-06-28. Brilliant succinct wisdom on creativity from an artist. Seth Godin says, "Hugh harangues and encourages and pushes and won't sit still until you, like him, are unwilling to settle." I highly recommend this to all musicians, artists, and entrepreneurs. Even those that prefer not to read much. :-)

title: Tribes
author: Seth Godin
context: Tribes - by Seth Godin Recommend it: 8/10. Date read: 2008-11-17. Inspiring look at what it takes to organize and mobilize groups of people.

title: How to Talk to Anyone
author: Leil Lowndes
context: How to Talk to Anyone - by Leil Lowndes Recommend it: 8/10. Date read: 2008-09-12. Wonderful considerate book about conversational people skills. (Warning: it’s written in an extremely flowery style, but try to see past that to get to the good stuff.) Gives specific instructions that are really useful for people who are not naturals. Just do what this book says, and people will warm up to you.

title: Brain Rules
author: John Medina
context: Brain Rules - by John Medina Recommend it: 8/10. Date read: 2008-08-26. New scientific insights into why our brains work this way, and how to use what we now know to learn or work better.

title: You, Inc - The Art of Selling Yourself
author: Harry Beckwith
context: You, Inc - The Art of Selling Yourself - by Harry Beckwith Recommend it: 8/10. Date read: 2008-07-26. One of my favorite authors, and a massive inspiration for my e-book. This is his newest, but read anything he’s done. It’s all top-notch insights on making life easier by being more considerate, whether you call that marketing or just life.

title: The Innovator’s Solution
author: Clayton Christensen
context: The Innovator’s Solution - by Clayton Christensen Recommend it: 8/10. Date read: 2006-09-21. Required reading for business-owners and investors. Shows how technology improves faster than people's ability to use it, so when someone says a technology is “not good enough”, add “yet” and prepare for disruption.

title: Small is the New Big
author: Seth Godin
context: Small is the New Big - by Seth Godin Recommend it: 8/10. Date read: 2006-09-08. I’m a massive fan and disciple. A collection of his short insightful posts from his blog, all thought-provoking and inspiring for anybody marketing anything, even music.

title: The 48 Laws of Power
author: Robert Greene and Joost Elffers
context: The 48 Laws of Power - by Robert Greene and Joost Elffers Recommend it: 8/10. Date read: 2003-05-06. Warning: some think this book is pure evil. But power exists, so it can only help to understand it better, even if you choose not to wield it.

title: Turkey - Culture Smart
author: Charlotte McPherson
context: Turkey - Culture Smart - by Charlotte McPherson Recommend it: 7/10. Date read: 2026-08-11. Türkiye history and cultural understanding. One of the better books in this series. The history helps explain today’s secular/religious balance or divisions. Then manners and travel tips.

title: You Can Just Do Things
author: Cate Hall and Sasha Chapin
context: You Can Just Do Things - by Cate Hall and Sasha Chapin Recommend it: 7/10. Date read: 2026-04-26. How to be agentic - to take charge and make things happen, no matter how unusual or uncomfortable it may be. Make your world the way you ideally want it to be, instead of normal. Cate Hall embodies this, so it’s great to hear it from someone really living it instead of just writing about it.

title: Nineteen Ways of Looking at Consciousness
author: Patrick House
context: Nineteen Ways of Looking at Consciousness - by Patrick House Recommend it: 7/10. Date read: 2026-04-08. Using the story of Anna - the patient who laughed when the surgeon stimulated parts of her brain - the author looks at the subject of consciousness from 19 different angles, writing in slightly different styles. He used the format of another book I have notes on here, titled “Nineteen Ways of Looking at Wang Wei”. Some beautiful poetic writing here.

title: Art of Spending Money
author: Morgan Housel
context: Art of Spending Money - by Morgan Housel Recommend it: 7/10. Date read: 2025-12-05. Philosophical thoughts on what to do with your money, which then relates to happiness, independence, envy, scarcity, and more. Putting money into savings is like buying independence. Imagine a 5-star chef cooks the most amazing meals for you 3× a day, every day. You’d lose the joy of a great meal since it’s no longer scarce. Implications for life?

title: Cosmopolitanism
author: Kwame Anthony Appiah
context: Cosmopolitanism - by Kwame Anthony Appiah Recommend it: 7/10. Date read: 2025-09-28. So many interesting ideas and questions about relativism, beliefs vs desires, openness, authenticity, pluralism.

title: Breakneck
author: Dan Wang
context: Breakneck - by Dan Wang Recommend it: 7/10. Date read: 2025-08-25. China is an engineering state, relentlessly pursuing megaprojects, while the United States has stalled because it’s transformed into a lawyerly society, reflexively blocking everything, good and bad.

title: Battleground: 10 Conflicts that Explain the New Middle East
author: Christopher Phillips
context: Battleground: 10 Conflicts that Explain the New Middle East - by Christopher Phillips Recommend it: 7/10. Date read: 2025-08-18. Summary of what’s been going on in West Asia since the 2011 Arab Spring. Great example of one book keeping you more informed than a hundred hours of daily news, since the book can summarize what was important in hindsight, showing outcomes and connections with what influenced or was influenced.

title: Heirs to Forgotten Kingdoms: the Disappearing Religions of the Middle East
author: Gerard Russell
context: Heirs to Forgotten Kingdoms: the Disappearing Religions of the Middle East - by Gerard Russell Recommend it: 7/10. Date read: 2025-08-11. The subtitle says it best: “Journeys into the Disappearing Religions of the Middle East”. British author, fluent in Arabic and Farsi, goes deep into Iraq, Iran, Lebanon, Egypt, and Pakistan to meet Mandaeans, Yazidis, Zoroastrians, Druze, Samaritans, Copts, and Kalasha. Fascinating bold anthropological adventure with insights into religion and history.

title: Voters as Mad Scientists
author: Bryan Caplan
context: Voters as Mad Scientists - by Bryan Caplan Recommend it: 7/10. Date read: 2025-07-15. Fun philosophical essays about political irrationality. I love the way he thinks, so I'm happy to read his thoughts on almost anything, just to hear his thought process.

title: The Myth of the Rational Voter
author: Bryan Caplan
context: The Myth of the Rational Voter - by Bryan Caplan Recommend it: 7/10. Date read: 2025-07-03. A critical look at democracy. I love the way he thinks so it’s fun to hear his thought process even though I’m not that interested in this subject.

title: Labor Econ Versus the World
author: Bryan Caplan
context: Labor Econ Versus the World - by Bryan Caplan Recommend it: 7/10. Date read: 2025-07-02. Good collection of philosopical essays around governance of labor and jobs. I love the way he thinks so it’s fun to hear his thought process even though I’m not that interested in this subject.

title: How Evil Are Politicians?
author: Bryan Caplan
context: How Evil Are Politicians? - by Bryan Caplan Recommend it: 7/10. Date read: 2025-06-27. Little essays of empathetic economics doggedly applied to topics around governance. Such a clear thinker. I love how he thinks, and how it inspires me to think and write too.

title: Wish Lanterns / China’s New Youth
author: Alec Ash
context: Wish Lanterns / China’s New Youth - by Alec Ash Recommend it: 7/10. Date read: 2024-11-24. 20-something British author living in Beijing got to know six Chinese people his own age, and profiled them deeply here through age 30, through 2016. Feels almost like fiction, following each character’s inner and outer life, switching between the six people in stages. If you feel that wide cultural profiles are too broad, and miss the personal touch, this format and writing is great.

title: River Town
author: Peter Hessler
context: River Town - by Peter Hessler Recommend it: 7/10. Date read: 2024-11-06. Memoir of an American 27-year-old spending two years teaching English in a small city in Western China from 1996-1998. Interesting to watch his progression of getting more comfortable there.

title: Hold On to Your Kids
author: Gordon Neufeld and Gabor Maté
context: Hold On to Your Kids - by Gordon Neufeld and Gabor Maté Recommend it: 7/10. Date read: 2024-09-16. Great parenting insights, mostly around the importance of the guiding relationship between parent and child, without which they seek attachment from friends who are less capable guides.

title: Unboxing Bengaluru
author: Malini Goyal and Prashanth Prakash
context: Unboxing Bengaluru - by Malini Goyal and Prashanth Prakash Recommend it: 7/10. Date read: 2024-08-20. I already love Bangalore, India, and plan to live there. But this is a good book that shows what’s wonderful about Bangalore, according to many of its residents and observers. I highly recommend to anyone interested.

title: The Stoic Challenge
author: William B. Irvine
context: The Stoic Challenge - by William B. Irvine Recommend it: 7/10. Date read: 2024-07-20. Ah, one of my favorite life philosophies. His previous book introduced me to Stoicism. This book elaborates on the idea with a specific angle of thinking of yourself as being tested, and to create challenging situations for yourself.

title: Israel: the Misunderstood Country
author: Noa Tishby
context: Israel: the Misunderstood Country - by Noa Tishby Recommend it: 7/10. Date read: 2023-08-20. History of modern country of Israel, written by someone whose grandparents were part of its founding. Unapologetically pro-Israel, but also pro-Palestine and anti-Hamas. Well-written though the occasional unnecessary adjectives (“horrific” / “brave”) remind you that it’s clearly biased and personal. Despite that, it’s really a great history book, riveting throughout.

title: Swisstory, History of Switzerland
author: Laurie Theurer
context: Swisstory, History of Switzerland - by Laurie Theurer Recommend it: 7/10. Date read: 2023-07-03. Great succinct history of Switzerland. Written and illustrated for kids, but really a perfect-sized quick read. It answered most of the questions I had in my recent visit.

title: Useful Delusions
author: Shankar Vedantam
context: Useful Delusions - by Shankar Vedantam Recommend it: 7/10. Date read: 2023-06-04. Same subject as my upcoming “Useful Not True” book, and so good I could almost recommend you read this instead. Almost. No massive epiphanies but many good points around the subject compiled in one place makes for a good argument. If you like “Useful Not True”, read this next.

title: Outlive
author: Peter Attia
context: Outlive - by Peter Attia Recommend it: 7/10. Date read: 2023-05-10. Expert advice on how to stay healthy into middle and old age. First half of the book was fluff for context. Second half was great specific advice. In short: exercise as much as an athlete.

title: Nietzsche: a complete introduction
author: Roy Jackson
context: Nietzsche: a complete introduction - by Roy Jackson Recommend it: 7/10. Date read: 2022-08-07. Clear summary and explanation of Nietzsche’s writing. I’ve listened to a whole audio course on Nietzsche and read another summary of his philosophy, but this book explains it best.

title: What Everyone Needs to Know about Islam
author: John L. Esposito
context: What Everyone Needs to Know about Islam - by John L. Esposito Recommend it: 7/10. Date read: 2022-07-13. Great clear introduction to Islam in an FAQ format. Common question, simple answer. Common question, simple answer. Almost every question was one I had considered once, but never actually asked. The book is not deep — just a high-level overview, which I found useful and fascinating.

title: Almost Perfect
author: Erika Lemay
context: Almost Perfect - by Erika Lemay Recommend it: 7/10. Date read: 2022-07-01. Elite athlete and physical artist shares her philosophy and actions that made her the best in the world. Wonderful intensity, focus, discipline, and ambition. Exciting and useful to hear her mindset, Übermensch in action, to apply to your own life and work.

title: The Courage to Be Happy
author: Ichiro Kishimi and Fumitake Koga
context: The Courage to Be Happy - by Ichiro Kishimi and Fumitake Koga Recommend it: 7/10. Date read: 2022-06-01. The sequel to the great “Courage to be Disliked”. The philosophy of Alfred Adler, on education, self-reliance, coming to terms with your past, focusing on solutions instead of problems, and active loving. Be warned, the format is strange: a dialog between an angry youth and calm philosopher. You can skim over what the youth says, since it's just angry objections.

title: Essays and Aphorisms
author: Arthur Schopenhauer
context: Essays and Aphorisms - by Arthur Schopenhauer Recommend it: 7/10. Date read: 2022-05-06. Classic philosophy. I strongly disagreed with his thoughts on the meaning of life, on women, and some on religion. But the rest were fascinating and worthy of deeper reflection. Too much to summarize. See notes.

title: Wanting
author: Luke Burgis
context: Wanting - by Luke Burgis Recommend it: 7/10. Date read: 2022-02-27. Pop explanation of René Girard’s anthropology of mimetic theory. We all imitate, but are rarely aware of it. Many relatable examples, though not a clear takeaway.

title: Beyond Order
author: Jordan Peterson
context: Beyond Order - by Jordan Peterson Recommend it: 7/10. Date read: 2022-02-10. Deep philosophy. Interesting voice. Great uncommon insights. Jungian. Brings almost any topic back to stories. Story of Pinnochio, stories in the Bible, story of your life. Stresses the importance of convention and social norms. 1st chapter had me talking about this book with friends immediately, loving it. 2nd chapter onwards, it was a tougher read. Needs a ruthless editor.

title: The Art of Creative Thinking
author: Rod Judkins
context: The Art of Creative Thinking - by Rod Judkins Recommend it: 7/10. Date read: 2022-01-29. 89 little inspiring thoughts and observations around the creative process written by someone who’s been in the thick of it for decades

title: Will
author: Will Smith and Mark Manson
context: Will - by Will Smith and Mark Manson Recommend it: 7/10. Date read: 2021-12-02. I loved this so much I couldn’t stop, and read in one sitting for 8 hours straight. I love autobiographies that distill lessons from their success. Similar to “Total Recall” by Schwarzenegger. I love reading the mindsets of the super-ambitious. Knowing Mark Manson’s writing so well, it’s fascinating to notice where it subtly changes voice from Will to Mark. Great insights. Really an ideal autobiography.

title: Cognitive Behavioral Therapy for Dummies
author: Rob Willson and Rhena Branch
context: Cognitive Behavioral Therapy for Dummies - by Rob Willson and Rhena Branch Recommend it: 7/10. Date read: 2020-09-22. If you haven’t looked into cognitive behavioral therapy, please do. It’s a clunky name but a great mindset. My notes here will give you an idea of what it’s about. It’s very effective for depression, anxiety, and more.

title: The Complacent Class
author: Tyler Cowen
context: The Complacent Class - by Tyler Cowen Recommend it: 7/10. Date read: 2019-11-06. America’s dynamic ever-changing past is slowing into a complacent stagnation. People don’t move as much or expect change. This hurts class mobility, and eventually needs to change. Inspired by his visit to China, which has grown 10% every year for 30 years, meaning every 7 years it’s like a whole new country is built. America is relatively halted.

title: Prisoners of Geography
author: Tim Marshall
context: Prisoners of Geography - by Tim Marshall Recommend it: 7/10. Date read: 2019-10-15. The world's cultures and politics are this way because of geography : oceans, rivers, mountains, deserts, farmable land, etc. Fascinating for me because I'd never looked at this world this way before.

title: Finland Culture Shock
author: Deborah Swallow
context: Finland Culture Shock - by Deborah Swallow Recommend it: 7/10. Date read: 2019-10-05. Surprisingly insightful. Much better than expected. An outsider’s insights into Finnish culture. I read it on my way to Finland, and swooned at the description of what sound like my kind of people. My experience in Finland mostly matches the book’s description, except I was in louder central Helsinki, so the anti-social silence was not on display. The book has a list of spectrums of culture which could be a good framework to categorize various countries’ cultures.

title: The Alter Ego Effect
author: Todd Herman
context: The Alter Ego Effect - by Todd Herman Recommend it: 7/10. Date read: 2019-06-15. Great idea: that you should create an inner hero that you bring out when performing. Athletes do this: when they compete they are “The Ghost Panther” (or whatever) in their mind, not their normal self. I’ve done and prescribed this for 20 years, so it’s cool to read a book on the subject. The point is simple. The book is filled with many anecdotes.

title: Life 3.0
author: Max Tegmark
context: Life 3.0 - by Max Tegmark Recommend it: 7/10. Date read: 2019-03-15. A deep, bold, and visionary dive into Artificial Intelligence and its many implications. One of the most interesting books I've ever read. If you haven't read much of AI yet, start with “Surviving AI” as an intro, then read this as a deep-dive. His perspective is amazingly thorough. Defining terminology was a great way to start. For example life is a “process that can retain its complexity and replicate”. Intelligence is the “ability to accomplish complex goals”. That keeps it broad enough to define future technology as alive and intelligent.

title: The Consolations of Philosophy
author: Alain De Botton
context: The Consolations of Philosophy - by Alain De Botton Recommend it: 7/10. Date read: 2018-08-28. How can the lessons of philosophers change your life? Thoughtful, unique, and funny book (cute illustrations) with some insightful ideas around that.

title: The Lessons of History
author: Will and Ariel Durant
context: The Lessons of History - by Will and Ariel Durant Recommend it: 7/10. Date read: 2018-04-25. They wrote the massive 11-volume 10,000-page “Story of Civilization” covering Western history, then wrote this tiny 100-page book succinctly summing up its lessons for our present day.

title: When
author: Daniel Pink
context: When - by Daniel Pink Recommend it: 7/10. Date read: 2018-04-17. A quick, entertaining, and informative book focusing on the effects of timing on your life. All points are kept extremely practical and applicable to life and job/work.

title: Perennial Seller
author: Ryan Holiday
context: Perennial Seller - by Ryan Holiday Recommend it: 7/10. Date read: 2017-12-06. Great thoughts on creating a timeless masterpiece (whether music, book, or any art) - and then promoting it. Very inspiring for any creator.

title: Principles
author: Ray Dalio
context: Principles - by Ray Dalio Recommend it: 7/10. Date read: 2017-10-07. Wow. So dense with wisdom that I wanted to highlight almost every paragraph. Instead, I skipped Part 1, about his background, because in the intro he recommends you skip it. I also skipped Part 3, about work principles, since they were all collaborative group-stuff, and I’m not working with anyone now. So here are my notes just from Part 2, “Life Principles”, which were so good I’ll probably re-read this book again next year. Caveat: it’s mostly so high-level — (“Decide what is true, then decide what to do about it.”) — that they’re more like koans to spark your own thoughts, instead of specific “do this” type advice.

title: How to Read a Book
author: Charles Van Doren and Mortimer Adler
context: How to Read a Book - by Charles Van Doren and Mortimer Adler Recommend it: 7/10. Date read: 2017-06-10. Light? No. Serious. Very serious and scholarly. Advises to read books that are above your current ability. A very specific methodology is given. Read books twice, ask questions while reading, answer those questions, then summarize and criticize afterwards. The point is to grow up to the level of the author.

title: Grit
author: Angela Duckworth
context: Grit - by Angela Duckworth Recommend it: 7/10. Date read: 2016-09-10. Grit is her word for persistence, focus, endurance, and constant improvement. Great thoughts on this point. If interested in it, also read the books here about deliberate practice.

title: How to Talk So Kids Will Listen & Listen So Kids Will Talk
author: Adele Fabe and Elaine Mazlish
