context: How to Talk So Kids Will Listen & Listen So Kids Will Talk - by Adele Fabe and Elaine Mazlish Recommend it: 7/10. Date read: 2016-08-17. Great thoughts on acknowledging kids' feelings.

title: The Inevitable
author: Kevin Kelly
context: The Inevitable - by Kevin Kelly Recommend it: 7/10. Date read: 2016-06-30. What are today's technologies inevitably going to lead to? Great predictions. Half of it was super-inspiring, painting a vision of the future that made me want to jump on it. Half felt like “well, duh, obviously!” maybe because I'm already deep in it.

title: Peak: Secrets from the New Science of Expertise
author: Anders Ericsson
context: Peak: Secrets from the New Science of Expertise - by Anders Ericsson Recommend it: 7/10. Date read: 2016-05-20. After being quoted in many books, the guy who coined “deliberate practice”, and spent his career studying just that, finally writes his own take on it. But I've already loved “The Talent Code”, “The Little Book of Talent”, “Moonwalking with Einstein”, “Talent is Overrated”, and “Little Bets”, which are all about this same field. So I didn't get much new out of it, but if you haven't already read those, maybe start here at the horse's mouth.

title: Deep Work
author: Cal Newport
context: Deep Work - by Cal Newport Recommend it: 7/10. Date read: 2016-04-10. Crucial subject, dear to me: shutting out distractions for deep productive concentrated work. No huge surprises but great supporting thoughts. I liked the point of considering the downside of the internet, instead of only the positives.

title: The Geography of Genius
author: Eric Weiner
context: The Geography of Genius - by Eric Weiner Recommend it: 7/10. Date read: 2016-02-02. What made Athens, Florence, Hangzhou, Vienna, Calcutta, and Silicon Valley such creative centers? Author goes to each to find out, and dives into the subject of creativity in general. He's such a great writer, so insightful, and finds so many great points of view from the people he interviews. See his other book here “Geography of Bliss”. Equally brilliant.

title: The Truth
author: Neil Strauss
context: The Truth - by Neil Strauss Recommend it: 7/10. Date read: 2015-11-22. Deep look at romantic relationships. Neil’s autobiography of transformation from being a womanizing sex addict, through therapy, concluding with commitment to his girlfriend. But interlaced in his story are powerful lessons about relationships.

title: Writing Tools
author: Roy Peter Clark
context: Writing Tools - by Roy Peter Clark Recommend it: 7/10. Date read: 2015-11-05. Great advice on how to be a better writer. Unfortunately the author’s writing style is distracting. How strange to take advice from someone not taking it themselves. Like a drunk telling you not to drink. Right after reading this book I gave it a terrible rating because of that, but now I realize its points and advice (in my notes, below) are truly great.

title: Fluent Forever
author: Gabriel Wyner
context: Fluent Forever - by Gabriel Wyner Recommend it: 7/10. Date read: 2014-08-18. Forget Rosetta Stone, Pimsleur, and the rest. I really believe this is the best way to learn another language, by far. Using the most up-to-date techniques and insights, and a unique emphasis on getting the sounds correct first. It's not easy, but it's much more effective than any other program or guide. Highly recommended if you're serious, and ready to do it.

title: Geography of Time
author: Robert Levine
context: Geography of Time - by Robert Levine Recommend it: 7/10. Date read: 2014-08-03. Interesting look at how different cultures consider time in different ways.

title: Show Your Work
author: Austin Kleon
context: Show Your Work - by Austin Kleon Recommend it: 7/10. Date read: 2014-06-15. Short inspiring book about sharing your work online. Really healthy perspective. Makes me want to do it much more.

title: How to Learn a Foreign Language
author: Paul Pimsleur
context: How to Learn a Foreign Language - by Paul Pimsleur Recommend it: 7/10. Date read: 2014-06-05. Short, punchy, incredibly insightful and useful book about learning another language, especially for a first-timer. I've read a few books on the subject now, but this is the only one that spoke directly to my issues. Especially loved his points on the importance of sounds over words. Hint: a language that is written but not spoken is called a dead language.

title: Man’s Search for Meaning
author: Viktor Frankl
context: Man’s Search for Meaning - by Viktor Frankl Recommend it: 7/10. Date read: 2014-06-04. Powerful, deep, etc. First half describes life inside Auschwitz. Second half has powerful succinctly-said insights into the universal struggle. There's a reason this book has sold a billion copies.

title: Toilet Training in Less Than A Day
author: Nathan Azrin
context: Toilet Training in Less Than A Day - by Nathan Azrin Recommend it: 7/10. Date read: 2014-05-01. This method worked great for toilet-training my son at age 2. It really did work in one day.

title: Choose Yourself!
author: James Altucher
context: Choose Yourself! - by James Altucher Recommend it: 7/10. Date read: 2014-04-10. Anyone who likes my writing will probably LOVE his writing. We've got a very similar style and approach. I was smiling most of the way through, reading things I could have (and wish I would have) written myself. His vulnerability is so endearing.

title: Self Reliance
author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
context: Self Reliance - by Ralph Waldo Emerson Recommend it: 7/10. Date read: 2013-11-08. Pow! This punched me in the gut from page one. Takes a tiny effort to read the English of the 1840s, but what a reward. A masterpiece essay (manifesto?) on independence, non-conformity, and trusting oneself.

title: How to Fail at Almost Everything and Still Win Big
author: Scott Adams
context: How to Fail at Almost Everything and Still Win Big - by Scott Adams Recommend it: 7/10. Date read: 2013-10-28. Random assortment of life tips/hacks from the creator of Dilbert. Interesting common thread of making your life a system for increasing your odds at success. But I liked the random tips, too.

title: No B.S. Time Management for Entrepreneurs
author: Dan S. Kennedy
context: No B.S. Time Management for Entrepreneurs - by Dan S. Kennedy Recommend it: 7/10. Date read: 2012-10-05. Repeated message: Your time is precious. Know its value and don't work for less. Defend it against time-vampires. Be hard to reach. Make every minute count. Do only the valuable tasks. Good conventional wisdom.

title: The Power of Habit
author: Charles Duhigg
context: The Power of Habit - by Charles Duhigg Recommend it: 7/10. Date read: 2012-03-01. Great dissection and analysis of what creates habits, and the power of changing just one of three steps in the habit loop.

title: The Passionate Programmer
author: Chad Fowler
context: The Passionate Programmer - by Chad Fowler Recommend it: 7/10. Date read: 2012-01-15. Wonderful book about the art, craft, and passion of being a great computer programmer. Loved the analogies to being a musician: sight-reading, being the worst member of the band, understanding new styles of music, practicing just for improvement, etc.

title: Poke the Box
author: Seth Godin
context: Poke the Box - by Seth Godin Recommend it: 7/10. Date read: 2011-03-15. Awesome short manifesto about getting into the habit of starting things. Inspiring as hell. Go go go!

title: The 4-Hour Body
author: Tim Ferriss
context: The 4-Hour Body - by Tim Ferriss Recommend it: 7/10. Date read: 2010-12-18. Amazing book for anyone wanting to improve their body. Core concept is the “minimum effective dose”: the smallest dose that will produce a desired outcome. Anything beyond that is wasteful. This documents Tim's years-long pursuit of the minimum effective dose of everything, from weight loss to muscle-building. Related subjects include orgasm, sleep, and medical tourism.

title: Hackers & Painters
author: Paul Graham
context: Hackers & Painters - by Paul Graham Recommend it: 7/10. Date read: 2010-08-20. A collection of essays from one of the best. Loosely about intelligence, entrepreneurship, programming, and questioning norms. Many brilliant ideas and insights.

title: I Will Teach You To Be Rich
author: Ramit Sethi
context: I Will Teach You To Be Rich - by Ramit Sethi Recommend it: 7/10. Date read: 2010-03-23. An amazing book about consumer finance and a healthy approach to managing your money. If you are age 18-35, this is a must-read! My notes are scarce, so get the book. Even if over 35, you might find some good tips on lowering your fees on various services, and a good reminder of good savings practices.

title: Being Logical
author: D.Q. McInerny
context: Being Logical - by D.Q. McInerny Recommend it: 7/10. Date read: 2010-03-15. World getting too fuzzy and unreasonable? Watching too much TV? A good book on logic is a great antidote. I'd never read one before, so I don't know how to compare it to others, but I really loved the clear thinking and deep insights here.

title: Why Smart People Make Big Money Mistakes
author: Gilovich and Belsky
context: Why Smart People Make Big Money Mistakes - by Gilovich and Belsky Recommend it: 7/10. Date read: 2009-10-19. My favorite genre of book lately: clear examples of bugs in our brain: where our intuition is wrong. But this one focuses just on money issues. Loss aversion. Sunk cost fallacy. Confirmation bias. Anchoring. Etc. I love this stuff.

title: Management of the Absurd
author: Richard Farson
context: Management of the Absurd - by Richard Farson Recommend it: 7/10. Date read: 2009-04-14. Counter-intuitive lessons about management. Highly recommended for managers and leaders, but also teachers and parents.

title: CrowdSourcing
author: Jeff Howe
context: CrowdSourcing - by Jeff Howe Recommend it: 7/10. Date read: 2008-08-27. Great look at a different way of getting a project done: not outsourcing it to a person, but developing a system where thousands of people can contribute a little bit.

title: Predictably Irrational
author: Dan Ariely
context: Predictably Irrational - by Dan Ariely Recommend it: 7/10. Date read: 2008-08-11. My favorite type of book: pointing out and understanding all of the counter-intuitive things people do.

title: The Magic of Thinking Big
author: David Schwartz
context: The Magic of Thinking Big - by David Schwartz Recommend it: 7/10. Date read: 2008-07-26. A classic self-help book. Exactly what you'd expect. But very good.

title: The Ultimate Sales Machine
author: Chet Holmes
context: The Ultimate Sales Machine - by Chet Holmes Recommend it: 7/10. Date read: 2008-06-12. After reading E-Myth Revisited, this is the best book I’ve seen on how to turn it into real results, step-by-step. Not ambiguous. Very “do it like this”.

title: The Art of Learning
author: Josh Waitzkin
context: The Art of Learning - by Josh Waitzkin Recommend it: 7/10. Date read: 2008-05-30. Chess master becomes Tai Chi master, realizes his real genius is learning, and shares his insights and stories.

title: Wikinomics
author: Don Tapscott and Anthony Williams
context: Wikinomics - by Don Tapscott and Anthony Williams Recommend it: 7/10. Date read: 2008-04-23. Lessons learned from Wikipedia can be applied to most other businesses. How can you harness the spare-time or self-interest of thousands to build something better for everyone?

title: The Wisdom of Crowds
author: James Surowiecki
context: The Wisdom of Crowds - by James Surowiecki Recommend it: 7/10. Date read: 2008-04-16. Mind-blowing examples of how groups of diverse people acting independently are smarter than any one person in the group. Has huge implications for management, markets, decision-making, and more.

title: Meatball Sundae
author: Seth Godin
context: Meatball Sundae - by Seth Godin Recommend it: 7/10. Date read: 2007-12-30. Instead of asking how to use the new internet tools to support your existing business, ask how you can change your business to take best advantage of the new tools.

title: Don’t Make Me Think
author: Steve Krug
context: Don’t Make Me Think - by Steve Krug Recommend it: 7/10. Date read: 2007-08-08. The classic book of web usability. Required reading for anyone who makes websites.

title: On Looking: Eleven Walks with Expert Eyes
author: Alexandra Horowitz
context: On Looking: Eleven Walks with Expert Eyes - by Alexandra Horowitz Recommend it: 6/10. Date read: 2026-07-28. Author walks around the city - usually her New York City neighborhood - with 11 different experts in different fields. Geologist, artist, sound designer, physician, child, dog, and a blind woman. Each pointing out what she hadn’t noticed. You’ll learn lots of trivia from this, but it’s fun, and makes you want to walk around a city again to try to notice these things.

title: Writing for Emotional Impact
author: Karl Iglesias
context: Writing for Emotional Impact - by Karl Iglesias Recommend it: 6/10. Date read: 2026-05-22. About the craft of writing a great film screenplay. A bit tedious (with sloppy repetitive writing) but I always love these books for making me see the craft behind movies I know well, and pointing out how to use this craft to make better stories in any medium.

title: Islam Explained
author: Ahmad Rashid Salim
context: Islam Explained - by Ahmad Rashid Salim Recommend it: 6/10. Date read: 2025-07-14. On this subject, I preferred the book What Everyone Needs to Know about Islam but since I read that three years ago, I was ready for another refresher on the subject, as I'm spending time in Muslim countries.

title: Has China Won?
author: Kishore Mahbubani
context: Has China Won? - by Kishore Mahbubani Recommend it: 6/10. Date read: 2025-06-23. Singapore diplomat’s insights into the China-USA relationship. Very pro-China with sound reasoning.

title: New China Playbook
author: Keyu Jin
context: New China Playbook - by Keyu Jin Recommend it: 6/10. Date read: 2025-06-16. Look into China’s economy and government as of 2023. Good explanations and insights, but quite financially focused. For a broader perspective, read “China’s World View” by David Daokui Li.

title: Political Thought of Xi Jinping
author: Steve Tsang and Olivia Cheung
context: Political Thought of Xi Jinping - by Steve Tsang and Olivia Cheung Recommend it: 6/10. Date read: 2025-04-29. Shares the stated and implied policy of China’s president. Fascinating.

title: The Complete Idiot’s Guide to Game Theory
author: Edward Rosenthal Ph.D.
context: The Complete Idiot’s Guide to Game Theory - by Edward Rosenthal Ph.D. Recommend it: 6/10. Date read: 2024-12-21. Great introduction to the subject.

title: Age of Ambition in the new China
author: Evan Osnos
context: Age of Ambition in the new China - by Evan Osnos Recommend it: 6/10. Date read: 2024-11-18. Journalist in China for many years focuses on three aspects of ~2013 Chinese culture: money, truth, faith. The first section was especially interesting with good insights.

title: Harry Potter and the Methods of Rationality
author: Eliezer Yudkowsky
context: Harry Potter and the Methods of Rationality - by Eliezer Yudkowsky Recommend it: 6/10. Date read: 2024-10-21. Amazing premise, but wow could it use an editor. 122 chapters, 660K words! Often drones on and on. Great ideas inside the verbosity, though. Most importantly, I felt it improving my thought processes after reading.

title: Self-Help Is Like a Vaccine
author: Bryan Caplan
context: Self-Help Is Like a Vaccine - by Bryan Caplan Recommend it: 6/10. Date read: 2024-10-18. Collection of various essays from an interesting thinker with surprising perspectives. Read the notes for a sampling.

title: Excellent Advice for Living
author: Kevin Kelly
context: Excellent Advice for Living - by Kevin Kelly Recommend it: 6/10. Date read: 2023-07-18. Tiny sentences with deep wisdom unelaborated. Up to you to extract, reflect, and apply.

title: The Essentials of Hinduism
author: Swami Bhaskarananda
context: The Essentials of Hinduism - by Swami Bhaskarananda Recommend it: 6/10. Date read: 2023-02-09. If you want to learn about Hinduism, this is the best book I’ve found so far. That said, it’s still very confusing to me.

title: Delphi Complete Works of William James
author: William James
context: Delphi Complete Works of William James - by William James Recommend it: 6/10. Date read: 2023-01-21. Huge book compiling all of his writing and speaking, so I didn’t read everything but just the parts I needed for my own research on pluralism and pragmatism. And for that, it was worth it for his insights.

title: Introducing Pragmatism
author: Cornelis de Waal
context: Introducing Pragmatism - by Cornelis de Waal Recommend it: 6/10. Date read: 2022-11-11. Semi-academic introduction to philosophers in the pragmatism tradition. Not a light read, but some great insights and ideas in the quotes.

title: Pragmatism an Introduction
author: Michael Bacon
context: Pragmatism an Introduction - by Michael Bacon Recommend it: 6/10. Date read: 2022-11-06. Semi-academic introduction to philosophers in the pragmatism tradition. Not a light read, but some great insights and ideas in the quotes.

title: Japanese Mind
author: Roger Davies and Osamu Ikeno
context: Japanese Mind - by Roger Davies and Osamu Ikeno Recommend it: 6/10. Date read: 2022-10-20. Good description of the Japanese mindset and its origins.

title: River Out of Eden
author: Richard Dawkins
context: River Out of Eden - by Richard Dawkins Recommend it: 6/10. Date read: 2022-01-24. Biologist describes how evolution works, everything maximized for the gene’s survival. Includes related insights and analogies. I like his writing style.

title: Where Is My Flying Car?
author: J Storrs Hall
context: Where Is My Flying Car? - by J Storrs Hall Recommend it: 6/10. Date read: 2021-07-13. Incredibly ambitious and specific. Says we’d have flying cars and nanotech today, and all power should be nuclear, if not for misguided regulations.

title: The Box
author: Marc Levinson
context: The Box - by Marc Levinson Recommend it: 6/10. Date read: 2021-06-26. History of the shipping container, and how it affected the world economy. Also for ambitious entrepreneurs, Malcom McLean is a damn good role model. Great read.

title: Before We Go
author: Dan John
context: Before We Go - by Dan John Recommend it: 6/10. Date read: 2021-06-19. Collection of essays about fitness and weight lifting. I love all of Dan John's books. This one is one of his best. Nothing revolutionary. Just great reminders.

title: The Beginning of Infinity
author: David Deutsch
context: The Beginning of Infinity - by David Deutsch Recommend it: 6/10. Date read: 2021-06-10. For the first three chapters, I thought it might be the best book I've ever read. But then chapter four and onwards lost my interest. Still, its core idea is brilliant and wonderful — that if something is permitted by the laws of physics, then the only thing that can prevent it from being technologically possible is not knowing how. Progress is unbounded. We are at the very beginning of an infinitely long Enlightenment, and will eventually figure out everything.

title: The Art of Possibility
author: Rosamund and Benjamin Zander
context: The Art of Possibility - by Rosamund and Benjamin Zander Recommend it: 6/10. Date read: 2020-11-15. Leadership coach and famous orchestra conductor collaborate on a book about relationships, art, personal development, children, and practice. Somewhat scattered but had some really interesting ideas.

title: Pre-Suasion
author: Robert Cialdini
context: Pre-Suasion - by Robert Cialdini Recommend it: 6/10. Date read: 2019-07-23. An interesting look at a single topic: what someone encounters beforehand greatly affects the influence of what comes after. Priming.

title: Surviving AI
author: Calum Chace
context: Surviving AI - by Calum Chace Recommend it: 6/10. Date read: 2019-03-05. A good overview of Artificial Intelligence. If you know nothing about it, start here, then read “Life 3.0” afterwards.

title: How Not to Be Wrong
author: Jordan Ellenberg
context: How Not to Be Wrong - by Jordan Ellenberg Recommend it: 6/10. Date read: 2019-02-01. Mathematics as an extension of common sense. I'd like to go through this again, doing and thoroughly understanding all the examples. On the first read, I let it pass over me.

title: Die Empty
author: Todd Henry
context: Die Empty - by Todd Henry Recommend it: 6/10. Date read: 2018-12-01. Motivating thoughts on doing your work. Your work is the expression of your priorities. “Work” = creating value where it didn't previously exist. An interesting definition of three kinds of work: mapping, making, and meshing.

title: Surely You’re Joking, Mr. Feynman!
author: Richard Feynman
context: Surely You’re Joking, Mr. Feynman! - by Richard Feynman Recommend it: 6/10. Date read: 2018-08-25. Autobiographical stories. Fun anecdotes. But they give a great glimpse into an approach to life: Doubt, challenge, and most importantly: test everything. Experiment. See what happens in the real-world, not in-theory. Applied not just to science, but how ants find food, talking to strangers in bars, sketching portraits, and playing a shaker in a Brazilian band.

title: Never Split the Difference (Negotiating)
author: Chris Voss and Tahl Raz
context: Never Split the Difference (Negotiating) - by Chris Voss and Tahl Raz Recommend it: 6/10. Date read: 2018-07-04. Advanced book about negotiating. Serious hostage type stuff. For a lighter book on negotiation, read “You Can Negotiate Anything” by Herb Cohen.

title: Getting the Love You Want
author: Harville Hendrix
context: Getting the Love You Want - by Harville Hendrix Recommend it: 6/10. Date read: 2018-03-17. Legendary book about making relationships work, recommended by many. Main point is that we're looking for our partner to heal childhood wounds. A must-read if you're near the start of a serious relationship.

title: Homo Deus
author: Yuval Noah Harari
context: Homo Deus - by Yuval Noah Harari Recommend it: 6/10. Date read: 2017-10-22. Very interesting alternative perspective on life from a historian. Anti-religion, anti-humanism, pro-animal. Seems detached, but is quite opinionated. Much to think about, regardless. My notes here give a taste. A lot to think about.

title: How to Live
author: Sarah Bakewell
context: How to Live - by Sarah Bakewell Recommend it: 6/10. Date read: 2017-10-02. A great biography of the original essayist Michel de Montaigne from the 1500’s, it also explores his philosophical questions. I loved learning about Pyrrhonian Skepticism.

title: Nobody Wants to Read Your Shit
author: Steven Pressfield
context: Nobody Wants to Read Your Shit - by Steven Pressfield Recommend it: 6/10. Date read: 2016-07-28. About the technique of writing stories. Good for what it is, but note it's not part of the War of Art series.

title: Living Beautifully with Uncertainty and Change
author: Pema Chödrön
context: Living Beautifully with Uncertainty and Change - by Pema Chödrön Recommend it: 6/10. Date read: 2016-04-20. Everything she writes is wonderful. All a similar theme. See the other books here for other (maybe better) examples.

title: Give and Take
author: Adam M. Grant
context: Give and Take - by Adam M. Grant Recommend it: 6/10. Date read: 2014-02-10. If you feel you are too generous, or too greedy, or are wary and insist on reciprocation, consider reading this research-based look at the subject of these different personality types. Counter-intuitive findings.

title: The Bed of Procrustes
author: Nassim Nicholas Taleb
context: The Bed of Procrustes - by Nassim Nicholas Taleb Recommend it: 6/10. Date read: 2014-01-15. I'm thrilled if I get a few counter-intuitive thought-provoking ideas from any source. This book is filled with his usual cocktail party sprezzatura bravado, but refreshingly succinct, minus his usual blowhard explanations of his superior scholarly approach to life.

title: Making Ideas Happen
author: Scott Belsky
context: Making Ideas Happen - by Scott Belsky Recommend it: 6/10. Date read: 2013-12-20. The full title - “Making Ideas Happen: Overcoming the Obstacles Between Vision and Reality” - describes its contents perfectly. Great book on that subject.

title: A Short History of Nearly Everything
author: Bill Bryson
context: A Short History of Nearly Everything - by Bill Bryson Recommend it: 6/10. Date read: 2013-08-25. Fun read of everything from the big bang to tectonic plates to the evolution of early man.

title: Ikigai
author: Sebastian Marshall
context: Ikigai - by Sebastian Marshall Recommend it: 6/10. Date read: 2013-07-06. Essays on history, power, self-discipline, negotiation, and the hustle. I especially liked his philosophy on luck, building universally valuable skills, and producing/shipping something from even fleeting interests.

title: Wired for Story
author: Lisa Cron
context: Wired for Story - by Lisa Cron Recommend it: 6/10. Date read: 2012-11-18. If you've read other books on how to write a great story, this probably won't hold much new for you. But this was my first book on this subject, and I loved it. Changed the way I pay attention to movies and novels. Makes me want to write a novel.

title: Pragmatic Programmer
author: Andy Hunt and David Thomas
context: Pragmatic Programmer - by Andy Hunt and David Thomas Recommend it: 6/10. Date read: 2012-09-27. Classic book for computer programmers. I read it first in 2003 before I was taking book notes, so I read it again now to take notes. Great wisdom in here. Amazing to see how much of its advice was adopted as norms by Ruby on Rails.

title: Meditations
author: Marcus Aurelius and C Scot Hicks and David V Hicks
context: Meditations - by Marcus Aurelius and C Scot Hicks and David V Hicks Recommend it: 6/10. Date read: 2012-02-04. A true classic, filled with stoic wisdom mostly about being your best rational self, doing good for its own sake, and not letting other people upset you.

title: The Developing World
author: Fredrik Härén
context: The Developing World - by Fredrik Härén Recommend it: 6/10. Date read: 2011-12-28. This is a wonderfully one-sided book that shows how exciting the big growth of China, India, Sri Lanka, Singapore, Myanmar, Malaysia, Indonesia, South Africa, Turkey, and Korea are. He's found great examples of people and companies doing really innovative things, but most of all it's a mindset.

title: You Are Not So Smart
author: David McRaney
context: You Are Not So Smart - by David McRaney Recommend it: 6/10. Date read: 2011-11-15. Great summary of 46 cognitive biases. Much of it covered in other books like Predictably Irrational, but if you haven't read those, this is a great starting book. Otherwise, just a good reminder, and worth reading.

title: The Lean Startup
author: Eric Ries
context: The Lean Startup - by Eric Ries Recommend it: 6/10. Date read: 2011-10-23. The methodology here is the one I recommend the most. The stuff I preach is like a cute casual intro to the real deal: the Lean Startup methodology. (As an aside: this book is the one that pushed my book out of the #1 slot on Amazon's Entrepreneur charts. Quite an honor.)

title: Seeking Wisdom
author: Peter Bevelin
context: Seeking Wisdom - by Peter Bevelin Recommend it: 6/10. Date read: 2011-01-03. A great overview of the lessons of Charlie Munger (partner of Warren Buffett) - and his approach to checklists of multi-disciplinary models to guide clear thinking. Main point: if you can just avoid mistakes, you're doing better than most. So it's a catalog of the most common or important mistakes. Focused on investing, but can be applied to life.

title: Start Small, Stay Small
author: Rob Walling and Mike Taber
context: Start Small, Stay Small - by Rob Walling and Mike Taber Recommend it: 6/10. Date read: 2010-11-16. Great how-to guide about being a micropreneur: an entrepreneur running many small but profitable businesses.

title: Making a Good Brain Great
author: Daniel G. Amen
context: Making a Good Brain Great - by Daniel G. Amen Recommend it: 6/10. Date read: 2010-07-28. About the care of the physical brain - the goo in your skull - from a doctor who scans brains and has linked specific behavior to brain chemistry.

title: On Writing
author: Stephen King
context: On Writing - by Stephen King Recommend it: 6/10. Date read: 2010-05-05. Great thoughts about writing (mostly books) from one of the most successful writers ever. Oddly doubles as an autobiography, telling many stories about his life from childhood.

title: Business Stripped Bare
author: Richard Branson
context: Business Stripped Bare - by Richard Branson Recommend it: 6/10. Date read: 2010-02-17. A real and specific description of the inner workings of the Virgin companies. Every entrepreneur, investor, and manager should appreciate this detailed account of practices, philosophies and stories from the core.

title: Talent Is Overrated
author: Geoff Colvin
context: Talent Is Overrated - by Geoff Colvin Recommend it: 6/10. Date read: 2009-11-16. Talent is not innate - it comes from thousands of hours of deliberate practice: focused improving of your shortcomings. That's it. If you can get past the first 20% of the book that just asks questions, the next 60% is quite good.

title: The Investor’s Manifesto
author: William J. Bernstein
context: The Investor’s Manifesto - by William J. Bernstein Recommend it: 6/10. Date read: 2009-11-12. Absolutely my favorite author and advisor on the subject of investing. Anyone with any money to invest (or already invested) please read this book. Such clear thinking, using only facts, and using numbers not guesses. Modern portfolio theory: use passive indexes of the entire market, no speculation, no stock picking, and avoid the entire fee-sucking financial industry.

title: Overachievement
author: John Eliot
context: Overachievement - by John Eliot Recommend it: 6/10. Date read: 2009-07-04. Performance coach, with a bent towards sports, surgery, and executive performance, gives his thoughts on being a top performer. The key is the "Trusting Mindset": like a squirrel runs across a telephone wire. Just doing it, without thought, because you've trained yourself plenty until that point.

title: The How of Happiness
author: Sonja Lyubomirsky
context: The How of Happiness - by Sonja Lyubomirsky Recommend it: 6/10. Date read: 2009-06-01. Since I loved Stumbling on Happiness, I was prepared to love this, but the big difference is that Stumbling on Happiness showed tests and experiments to prove their points, whereas this book only presents conclusions. Maybe equally accurate but less convincing.

title: Personal Development for Smart People
author: Steve Pavlina
context: Personal Development for Smart People - by Steve Pavlina Recommend it: 6/10. Date read: 2008-12-27. A broad look at all different aspects of self-improvement. Some unique insights. But it's based on this abstract pyramid of power/love/oneness stuff that I couldn't relate to. Though inbetween those lie some great concrete ideas.

title: The Culture Code
author: Clotaire Rapaille
context: The Culture Code - by Clotaire Rapaille Recommend it: 6/10. Date read: 2008-11-01. Weird look at how different cultures (mostly Europe versus U.S. in this book) see things differently. Example: British luxury is about detachment whereas U.S. luxury is about rank.

title: The Four Pillars of Investing
author: William Bernstein
context: The Four Pillars of Investing - by William Bernstein Recommend it: 6/10. Date read: 2008-06-07. If you've already read and loved The Smartest Investment Book You'll Ever Read, above, then read this more in-depth book next.

title: Here Comes Everybody
author: Clay Shirky
context: Here Comes Everybody - by Clay Shirky Recommend it: 6/10. Date read: 2008-04-06. Like Wikinomics and Crowdsourcing, required reading if interested in harnessing the collective power of people online.

title: The Culting of Brands
author: Douglas Atkin
context: The Culting of Brands - by Douglas Atkin Recommend it: 6/10. Date read: 2008-02-08. Unique fascinating dissection of cults and why they work. Then how to apply those lessons to marketing your business.

title: Made to Stick
author: Chip Heath and Dan Heath
context: Made to Stick - by Chip Heath and Dan Heath Recommend it: 6/10. Date read: 2007-03-12. Actually analyzing what makes certain ideas or stories more memorable than others! Fascinating. Apply this wisdom to your songs, bio/story, communication with fans, etc.

title: Maximum Achievement
author: Brian Tracy
context: Maximum Achievement - by Brian Tracy Recommend it: 6/10. Date read: 2006-11-12. A classic self-help book. Exactly what you'd expect. I don't agree with all of it.

title: China in Ten Words
author: Yu Hua 余华
context: China in Ten Words - by Yu Hua 余华 Recommend it: 5/10. Date read: 2026-03-14. Famous fiction author. I loved the movie from his book “To Live”. Memoir of growing up in China filtered through ten topics. Sometimes it’s cultural insights, but sometimes just his personal stories. Deep insights on “copycat” and “bamboozle”. Note those words are rough English translations of the real Chinese words he’s discussing.

title: Existentialism: A Beginner’s Guide
author: Thomas Wartenberg
context: Existentialism: A Beginner’s Guide - by Thomas Wartenberg Recommend it: 5/10. Date read: 2026-01-05. Light introduction to Existentialism. Points to some more important works, and gives some context. Good information and insights but written in a style that was hard for me to parse. Happy to now have my notes here after much editing.

title: Rule Makers, Rule Breakers
author: Michele Gelfand
context: Rule Makers, Rule Breakers - by Michele Gelfand Recommend it: 5/10. Date read: 2025-11-30. Asks the question I love: Why are different cultures that way? Focuses particularly on strict versus loose cultures, hence the title. Some of its answers were insightful, but others feel dead wrong and easy to disprove. Still, a worthy read for the good bits. I liked that they used New Zealand as a frequent example.

title: Vagabonding
author: Rolf Potts
context: Vagabonding - by Rolf Potts Recommend it: 5/10. Date read: 2025-11-05. I read it long after release, when its ideas are thoroughly ingested into my culture, so it had few surprises. I prefer his newer “Vagabond’s Way”.

title: Knowledge, Reality, and Value
author: Michael Huemer
context: Knowledge, Reality, and Value - by Michael Huemer Recommend it: 5/10. Date read: 2025-08-01. Perfect introduction to academic philosophy. Real philosopher’s definitions. Differs from the more self-help style philosophy I love. Great examples of clear thinking.

title: Connecting the Dots
author: Sam Brinson
context: Connecting the Dots - by Sam Brinson Recommend it: 5/10. Date read: 2024-11-28. About learning. I would have loved it, but I'd already read all the sources it got its information from, so unfortunately it was nothing new to me.

title: In This Economy?
author: Kyla Scanlon
context: In This Economy? - by Kyla Scanlon Recommend it: 5/10. Date read: 2024-09-05. Economics explained for non-economists. Highly recommended if that’s what you want.

title: SuperBetter
author: Jane McGonigal
context: SuperBetter - by Jane McGonigal Recommend it: 5/10. Date read: 2024-08-17. I was excited to read a book about living gamefully, so I bought it, then found out it was more about recovery - using this approach to heal from trauma. I will read it again with more interest when I have trauma.

title: Linguistics: A Complete Introduction
author: David Hornsby
context: Linguistics: A Complete Introduction - by David Hornsby Recommend it: 5/10. Date read: 2024-08-10. Lessons in linguistics for beginning students of the subject.

title: Chile Culture Smart
author: Caterina Perrone
context: Chile Culture Smart - by Caterina Perrone Recommend it: 5/10. Date read: 2024-06-02. Basic information in preparation for travel.

title: Argentina Culture Smart
author: Mary Godward and Robert Hamwee
context: Argentina Culture Smart - by Mary Godward and Robert Hamwee Recommend it: 5/10. Date read: 2024-05-22. Basic information in preparation for travel.

title: Colombia Culture Smart
author: Kate Cathey
context: Colombia Culture Smart - by Kate Cathey Recommend it: 5/10. Date read: 2024-05-19. Basic information in preparation for travel.

title: Mexico Culture Smart
author: Russell Maddicks
context: Mexico Culture Smart - by Russell Maddicks Recommend it: 5/10. Date read: 2024-05-17. Basic information in preparation for travel.

title: This Is Mexico
author: Carol Merchasin
context: This Is Mexico - by Carol Merchasin Recommend it: 5/10. Date read: 2024-05-15. Day-to-day insights from an American lawyer who moved to Mexico. Read in preparation for travel.

title: Persuasion Story Code
author: David Garfinkel
context: Persuasion Story Code - by David Garfinkel Recommend it: 5/10. Date read: 2024-02-09. About stories meant to sell something. You say to the waiter, “Tell me about the filet.” You’re asking for a tiny story. Most of our desires come with a little story of explanation or persuasion. Interesting subject, and the author is a super-expert on the subject.

title: The Power of Regret
author: Daniel Pink
context: The Power of Regret - by Daniel Pink Recommend it: 5/10. Date read: 2023-11-25. You won’t say “no regrets” again. Regret’s usefulness in improving future decisions. But also a warning against the pursuit of regret minimizing. Deeper insights than I expected.

title: What’s in It for Them?
author: Joe Polish
context: What’s in It for Them? - by Joe Polish Recommend it: 5/10. Date read: 2023-02-11. I like Joe and love what he’s done with his Genius Network. The book is a good reminder of the importance of networking, and some insights from an expert.

title: Everything in Its Place (Work Clean)
author: Dan Charnas
context: Everything in Its Place (Work Clean) - by Dan Charnas Recommend it: 5/10. Date read: 2022-10-08. Mise-in-place. Chefs spend more time planning than actually cooking. The success of the kitchen depends on its processes. Apply this to your work.

title: How to Know Everything
author: Elke Wiss
context: How to Know Everything - by Elke Wiss Recommend it: 5/10. Date read: 2022-09-05. Really how to ask better questions. How to learn through conversational questioning and listening.

title: The Me, Me, Me Epidemic
author: Amy McCready
context: The Me, Me, Me Epidemic - by Amy McCready Recommend it: 5/10. Date read: 2022-01-15. Good parenting advice on how to prevent or cure entitlement. Take responsibility. Pay consequences. Very verbose and full of examples.

title: Attempts
author: Dan John
context: Attempts - by Dan John Recommend it: 5/10. Date read: 2021-06-17. I love his writing about fitness and strength. Nothing unconventional except his focus on the fundamentals and basics.

title: Consider This
author: Chuck Palahniuk
context: Consider This - by Chuck Palahniuk Recommend it: 5/10. Date read: 2020-10-03. Author of “Fight Club” with some thoughts and stories about writing and life. I read it looking only for thoughts on the craft of writing, but actually the stories and random insights were useful and interesting. (“What dogs want is for no one to ever leave.” “No two people ever walk into the same room.”)

title: Scepticism: A Very Short Introduction
author: Duncan Pritchard
context: Scepticism: A Very Short Introduction - by Duncan Pritchard Recommend it: 5/10. Date read: 2020-07-01. I love scepticism as a subject, as a mindset, raising the standards of knowledge or belief. Especially self-doubt: not believing yourself. This book was a bit too academic, but worthwhile with good ideas.

title: True Style
author: G. Bruce Boyer
context: True Style - by G. Bruce Boyer Recommend it: 5/10. Date read: 2020-04-04. A balanced, relaxed, healthy look at traditional men’s clothing by a long-time writer on the subject.

title: Brain Rules for Aging Well
author: John Medina
context: Brain Rules for Aging Well - by John Medina Recommend it: 5/10. Date read: 2019-01-05. I recommend this 10/10 if you're over 60, 8/10 if you're over 40, 4/10 otherwise. Current research on brain aging, and how to slow or reverse its effects. Be very social. Read 3+ hours per week. Intensely learn something new, especially a new language. Take dance lessons. Practice gratitude and mindfulness. Flood your mind with nostalgic memories.

title: The Artist’s Journey
author: Steven Pressfield
context: The Artist’s Journey - by Steven Pressfield Recommend it: 5/10. Date read: 2018-09-16. I love this series of books from him, from War of Art to Turning Pro. This is worth reading if you need a nudge on this subject, but if you've read the others, it only offers a little more.

title: Swiss Watching
author: Diccon Bewes
context: Swiss Watching - by Diccon Bewes Recommend it: 5/10. Date read: 2018-07-08. About the culture of Switzerland, written by a Brit. I love these kinds of country culture books, and have always been curious about Switzerland, so it scratched my itch, and has good insights. The description of how the government works was most interesting.

title: Mindfulness in Plain English
author: Henepola Gunaratana
context: Mindfulness in Plain English - by Henepola Gunaratana Recommend it: 5/10. Date read: 2018-05-25. Thoughts and instruction on Vipassana meditation, explained clearly.

title: How Music Works
author: David Byrne
context: How Music Works - by David Byrne Recommend it: 5/10. Date read: 2018-01-30. Some interesting historical perspectives I hadn't thought of, like how the venue's reverberation changed composition. Highlight for me was the Byrne/Eno creative thoughts on their approach to writing and recording music, which I've always loved.

title: The Way of the Linguist
author: Steve Kaufmann
context: The Way of the Linguist - by Steve Kaufmann Recommend it: 5/10. Date read: 2017-09-30. Written by someone who has learned many languages, he shares his story and advice. Useful recommendations.

title: Tools of Titans
author: Tim Ferriss
context: Tools of Titans - by Tim Ferriss Recommend it: 5/10. Date read: 2017-08-30. A very useful collection of notes from hundreds of hours of Tim's podcast interviews. It's definitely a mix of thoughts and advice from a mix of people. A real collage. The first quarter of the book, full of milligram measurements of things you could be ingesting, almost made me quit, but the 2nd half of the book had some great ideas.

title: Zero to One
author: Peter Thiel and Blake Masters
context: Zero to One - by Peter Thiel and Blake Masters Recommend it: 5/10. Date read: 2016-03-10. Brilliant, bold, and clear thoughts about how to make a big Silicon Valley size company. Other great insights like definite/indefinite optimism/pessimism.

title: How Adam Smith Can Change Your Life
author: Russ Roberts
context: How Adam Smith Can Change Your Life - by Russ Roberts Recommend it: 5/10. Date read: 2015-05-07. Adam Smith wrote “Theory of Moral Sentiments” in the 1700s. Now Russ puts it into modern language and times. Main point is that our morality comes from imagining being judged by our fellow man.

title: Daily Rituals: How Artists Work
author: Mason Currey
context: Daily Rituals: How Artists Work - by Mason Currey Recommend it: 5/10. Date read: 2014-08-15. Collections of the creative routines of famous writers, artists, musicians, and scientists. Some interesting insights, but mostly reinforcing proof that it's important to keep a daily routine to put aside time for your creative work.

title: The Story of French
author: Jean-Benoit Nadeau and Julie Barlow
context: The Story of French - by Jean-Benoit Nadeau and Julie Barlow Recommend it: 5/10. Date read: 2014-02-02. Just an interesting history and present look at the French language. I had no idea what an influence French was on English, and didn't understand its role in current Africa. Makes me want to learn French.

title: Island
author: Aldous Huxley
context: Island - by Aldous Huxley Recommend it: 5/10. Date read: 2013-12-14. This book totally changed my life at a key moment, when I was 22. It made me quit my job and pursue a life of variety. Some great ideas inside, especially the ones about family and healthy child-rearing. I just re-read it now, 22 years later, and it didn't hit me as hard as it did back then, maybe because I've internalized its philosophies so completely.

title: Ready for Anything
author: David Allen
context: Ready for Anything - by David Allen Recommend it: 5/10. Date read: 2013-11-28. I read this in 2004, before Getting Things Done (same author), and liked it more, because it's more philosophical than instructional. It made a big impact on me then. I was just re-reading now for a little refresher.

title: Starting Strength
author: Mark Rippetoe
context: Starting Strength - by Mark Rippetoe Recommend it: 5/10. Date read: 2013-11-01. For those who ever considered getting fit, this is the way to do it, and the best book on the subject. Not sure if I should put this in my book list, because it's not something you read, but something you do.

title: The Now Habit
author: Neil Fiore
context: The Now Habit - by Neil Fiore Recommend it: 5/10. Date read: 2013-04-05. Good book with insights and advice on overcoming procrastination.

title: Mastery
author: Robert Greene
context: Mastery - by Robert Greene Recommend it: 5/10. Date read: 2012-12-06. Mostly detailed historical biographical tales of ”masters” like DaVinci, Darwin, Mozart, Proust, Goethe, Wright Brothers, Einstein, Coltrane, Martha Graham, etc. Lessons dissected from their successes, and categorized. Similar format to his great book “48 Laws of Power”, but a little less effective here. The biographies were interesting, but lessons were mostly conventional wisdom.

title: Meditation for Beginners
author: Jack Kornfield
context: Meditation for Beginners - by Jack Kornfield Recommend it: 5/10. Date read: 2012-01-12. Just some nice thoughts on meditation.

title: Fail-Safe Investing
author: Harry Browne
context: Fail-Safe Investing - by Harry Browne Recommend it: 5/10. Date read: 2011-04-21. Its main point is the “Permanent Portfolio” - a beautiful simple idea to have 25% of your savings each in investments that do well during boom (stocks), bust (bonds), inflation (gold), deflation (cash). Then just rebalance when they get too far out of 25% each. No predicting the future. No worrying about the news. Just 25% each and rebalance.

title: Linchpin
author: Seth Godin
context: Linchpin - by Seth Godin Recommend it: 5/10. Date read: 2010-12-11. For someone who has a job at a company, I would call this essential reading with my highest recommendation. Since I haven't had a job since 1992, I couldn't apply many of his great points to my life. Still I loved his reminder of the value of the brilliant workers instead of systemized workers. The opposite of E-Myth (another book reviewed here).

title: Cognitive Surplus
author: Clay Shirky
context: Cognitive Surplus - by Clay Shirky Recommend it: 5/10. Date read: 2010-12-10. I always love Clay Shirky's insights into the internet culture. This is about how all the spare time people are using to add to Wikipedia or create YouTube videos is previously time they were passively watching TV. Perhaps passive watching was a temporary habit that lasted 80 years, and now we're going back to a more participatory culture?

title: The Selfish Gene
author: Richard Dawkins
context: The Selfish Gene - by Richard Dawkins Recommend it: 5/10. Date read: 2010-09-18. About evolution and the theory of natural selection, proposing the idea that it's not creatures that are looking to replicate, but individual genes.

title: Nudge
author: Richard Thaler and Cass Sunstein
context: Nudge - by Richard Thaler and Cass Sunstein Recommend it: 5/10. Date read: 2010-08-15. Introducing the idea of Libertarian Paternalism: influencing people's behavior for their own benefit, without forbidding any options or significantly changing their economic incentives.

title: Pragmatic Thinking and Learning
author: Andy Hunt
context: Pragmatic Thinking and Learning - by Andy Hunt Recommend it: 5/10. Date read: 2009-11-03. A great curated collection of facts about how to learn effectively and think clearly. Since it's written by a programmer, it makes many computer analogies that fellow programmers will appreciate. Non-programmers might feel a little left out.

title: The Great Formula
author: Mark Joyner
context: The Great Formula - by Mark Joyner Recommend it: 5/10. Date read: 2009-06-06. Create an irresistible offer. Present it to people who need it. Sell them more afterwards. Lots of examples of this.

title: Outliers: The Story of Success
author: Malcolm Gladwell
context: Outliers: The Story of Success - by Malcolm Gladwell Recommend it: 5/10. Date read: 2009-04-23. Deep study of why some people are so much more successful. Often due to circumstances and early opportunities, but really comes down to the fact that it takes about 10,000 hours of hard work to master something.

title: Lucky Or Smart?
author: Bo Peabody
context: Lucky Or Smart? - by Bo Peabody Recommend it: 5/10. Date read: 2009-04-23. Tiny book by an incredibly successful serial entrepreneur telling his tales and lessons learned.

title: The China Study
author: Campbell and Campbell
context: The China Study - by Campbell and Campbell Recommend it: 5/10. Date read: 2009-04-23. Biggest study ever on the effects of diet on health. The multiple health benefits of plant-based foods, and dangers of animal-based foods, including all types of meat, dairy and eggs.

title: The Power of Less
author: Leo Babauta
context: The Power of Less - by Leo Babauta Recommend it: 5/10. Date read: 2009-01-21. Identify the essential. Eliminate the rest. Set limitations. Become incredibly effective. Written by someone who's been successfully living this way for years.

title: Cut to the Chase
author: Stuart Levine
context: Cut to the Chase - by Stuart Levine Recommend it: 5/10. Date read: 2008-07-26. Tips on more effective communication.

title: Know-How
author: Ram Charan with Geri Willigan
context: Know-How - by Ram Charan with Geri Willigan Recommend it: 5/10. Date read: 2007-02-12. Acquired expertise in big business. Subtitle: 8 Skills That Separate People Who Perform from Those Who Don't.

title: The Art of Project Management
author: Scott Berkun
context: The Art of Project Management - by Scott Berkun Recommend it: 5/10. Date read: 2006-11-19. The best book on how to oversee projects to completion.

title: In Praise of Commercial Culture
author: Tyler Cowen
context: In Praise of Commercial Culture - by Tyler Cowen Recommend it: 4/10. Date read: 2025-11-24. Cultural optimism! I’d never considered that term before, but I love its mindset. My life was changed when Camille Paglia said, in the 90s, that Hollywood movies are the high art of our times. It enriched my life to see them that way ever since. Now in this book Tyler uses her statement as an example of cultural optimism. I see it in his day-to-day writing and podcasting too. I recommend this book for its focus on that, and great art/cutlure insights. But the book is 25 years old now, with expired references, and he’s improved so much as a writer since then.

title: No B.S. Ruthless Management of People and Profits
author: Dan Kennedy
context: No B.S. Ruthless Management of People and Profits - by Dan Kennedy Recommend it: 4/10. Date read: 2025-06-21. His cantakerous-old-man style is refreshing. Super pragmatic. I have no employees now so most of it was moot but it was a refreshing and slightly inspiring read.

title: Other Rivers
author: Peter Hessler
context: Other Rivers - by Peter Hessler Recommend it: 4/10. Date read: 2024-11-10. American who taught in China in 1997, then lived in Beijing for 10 years, returns to China - Chengdu - to teach in 2019 and notes the differences. But also happened to be there when COVID hit, so he shares what it was like in 2020-2021 there.

title: Nineteen Ways of Looking at Wang Wei
author: Eliot Weinberger
context: Nineteen Ways of Looking at Wang Wei - by Eliot Weinberger Recommend it: 4/10. Date read: 2024-04-27. Understanding the difficulty and importance of translation, by looking at 19 different translations of a single poem from the Tang Dynasty.

title: Arabian Sands
author: Wilfred Thesiger
context: Arabian Sands - by Wilfred Thesiger Recommend it: 4/10. Date read: 2024-01-03. Travel journal from 1946-1948, a bit tedious at its journaling parts, just saying where they went and what they did. But I read on for the occasional cultural insights into Arab culture, and I’m glad I did. My jaw dropped when he casually mentioned spending months staying with the great Zayed bin Sultan Al Nahyan in Abu Dhabi, who later became founder of United Arab Emirates.

title: Rebel Talent
author: Francesca Gino
context: Rebel Talent - by Francesca Gino Recommend it: 4/10. Date read: 2023-07-16. Insights into the connection between rule-breakers and innovation. Social norms, trust, novelty.

title: The Toilet Paper Entrepreneur
author: Mike Michalowicz
context: The Toilet Paper Entrepreneur - by Mike Michalowicz Recommend it: 4/10. Date read: 2023-06-10. Some thoughts on entrepreneurship. About being resourceful, scrappy, savvy. I like the focus on beliefs. Loved the $100 bill example.

title: Rich Dad Poor Dad
author: Robert Kiyosaki
context: Rich Dad Poor Dad - by Robert Kiyosaki Recommend it: 4/10. Date read: 2023-06-05. Not a great book, but communicates a very valuable mindset. I’m reading it to my son who wants to learn how to make money. Its simplistic and repeated message aims to get you out of the employee mindset, and to only spend your money on income-generating assets.

title: Pragmatism as a Way of Life
author: Ruth Anna and Hilary Putnam
context: Pragmatism as a Way of Life - by Ruth Anna and Hilary Putnam Recommend it: 4/10. Date read: 2023-05-20. Renowned philosphers and married couple. Her writing is clear and wonderful. But his? Every sentence is a tangled knot of side-clauses that made me stare at the page in confusion. I loved her description of moral skepticism even though I disagreed with her conclusions. I skipped most of his chapters and almost gave up on the book, but because of her chapters I’m glad I didn’t.

title: Loving What Is
author: Byron Katie
context: Loving What Is - by Byron Katie Recommend it: 4/10. Date read: 2022-12-01. Its wisdom is great, but its writing is absolutely awful. The book is mostly unedited transcripts of live group therapy sessions, including every little speech affectation, and lots of repetitive unnecessary rambling. But if you can get through all that, there are some great ideas inside of it, prompting you to question your harmful stories.

title: Essays One
author: Lydia Davis
context: Essays One - by Lydia Davis Recommend it: 4/10. Date read: 2022-10-15. Author talks about her methods, and the craft of writing.

title: Everything Is Obvious
author: Duncan Watts
context: Everything Is Obvious - by Duncan Watts Recommend it: 4/10. Date read: 2022-10-05. Common sense and intuition are often wrong. They are like mythology, good for explaining events with stories, but not for understanding. Some good insights here.

title: The Socrates Express
author: Eric Weiner
context: The Socrates Express - by Eric Weiner Recommend it: 4/10. Date read: 2022-06-02. An overview of 14 philosophers including some less-mentioned ones like Pillow Booth author Sei Shōnagon, and Mahatma Gandhi. I liked his other books, but this time his travels and personal commentary felt like an unrewarding distraction. But good overview of philosophies with some great observations inbetween.

title: The Data Detective
author: Tim Harford
context: The Data Detective - by Tim Harford Recommend it: 4/10. Date read: 2021-06-27. If you haven’t read books about statistics, this is a good fun overview. Unfortunately I have, so it was too familiar. And it’s written from the very-current world of media defensiveness, preparing you to argue and challenge media headlines. Not for me.

title: The Philosophy of Cognitive-Behavioural Therapy
author: Donald Robertson
context: The Philosophy of Cognitive-Behavioural Therapy - by Donald Robertson Recommend it: 4/10. Date read: 2020-09-24. After learning about Cognitive-Behavioural Therapy from the “… for Dummies” book, I wanted to see how it was applied to Stoicism. The book did not disappoint, and is a good reinforcement of the mindset.

title: The New York Nobody Knows
author: William Helmreich
context: The New York Nobody Knows - by William Helmreich Recommend it: 4/10. Date read: 2019-10-20. Fascinating if you want to get to know NYC better. Author walked every single block of every borough in New York City. 6000 miles. Talked with everyone he could along the way. Shares his experience and insights here.

title: Barking Up the Wrong Tree
author: Eric Barker
context: Barking Up the Wrong Tree - by Eric Barker Recommend it: 4/10. Date read: 2017-11-04. Some thoughts on success.

title: The Only Investment Guide You’ll Ever Need
author: Andrew Tobias
context: The Only Investment Guide You’ll Ever Need - by Andrew Tobias Recommend it: 4/10. Date read: 2016-05-02. Hm. Highly recommended, so maybe you'll love it. I've read many like this, so I only got a few good ideas from it. I preferred “The Smartest Investment Book You'll Ever Read” also here in my book list, for more punch per page.

title: Germany: Unraveling an Enigma
author: Greg Nees
context: Germany: Unraveling an Enigma - by Greg Nees Recommend it: 4/10. Date read: 2016-02-10. Written by an American who's lived in Germany for 20 years. Published in 2000, (and so probably written a couple years before), it's a little dated. The Berlin Wall was a fresh memory. So I'm assuming the current (for then) observations have changed a bit. But the historical perspective helped explain some core aspects to the culture.

title: Never Let Go
author: Dan John
context: Never Let Go - by Dan John Recommend it: 4/10. Date read: 2014-08-22. Some thoughts and advice on weight lifting and strength training.

title: In Pursuit of Silence
author: George Prochnik
context: In Pursuit of Silence - by George Prochnik Recommend it: 4/10. Date read: 2013-11-13. Interesting thoughts and findings on the search for peace and quiet in the modern world.

title: The Laws of Subtraction
author: Matthew May
context: The Laws of Subtraction - by Matthew May Recommend it: 4/10. Date read: 2013-01-09. I'm biased. I'm in it. This is a subject I live. So I flipped through a little fast, thinking, “Yep. I know. Got it. Living it. Yep.” But for those who need some minimalist inspiration, this has some great thoughts in it.

title: The 4-Hour Chef
author: Timothy Ferriss
context: The 4-Hour Chef - by Timothy Ferriss Recommend it: 4/10. Date read: 2012-11-20. Not about being a chef, but about learning itself. 672 pages long and I had a new baby at the time, so I didn't give this the attention it deserves.

title: Drop Dead Healthy
author: A. J. Jacobs
context: Drop Dead Healthy - by A. J. Jacobs Recommend it: 4/10. Date read: 2012-05-22. Funny and informative book by the always-brilliant A.J. Jacobs - about trying every health remedy and suggestion. Some surprising ones are effective.

title: Little Bets
author: Peter Sims
context: Little Bets - by Peter Sims Recommend it: 4/10. Date read: 2011-05-10. Examples of the fact that much success or creativity comes from trying many things, failing fast, getting feedback, trying more things, and deliberate practice. Stories from Pixar, Chris Rock, Silicon Valley, Frank Gehry.

title: One Simple Idea
author: Stephen Key
context: One Simple Idea - by Stephen Key Recommend it: 4/10. Date read: 2011-04-29. Good introduction into the world of licensing your ideas to companies that manufacture products.

title: Focus
author: Leo Babauta
context: Focus - by Leo Babauta Recommend it: 4/10. Date read: 2011-01-17. Nice short reminder of the importance of solitude and focus. Single-tasking. Only doing your most important things, and let the rest go.

title: The Upside of Irrationality
author: Dan Ariely
context: The Upside of Irrationality - by Dan Ariely Recommend it: 4/10. Date read: 2010-07-05. First read his amazing book “Predictably Irrational.” But if you read and loved it, then this is a continuation with some more examples - mostly organizational. He also catharticly details his own painful injuries in every chapter.

title: Confessions of a Public Speaker
author: Scott Berkun
context: Confessions of a Public Speaker - by Scott Berkun Recommend it: 4/10. Date read: 2010-06-28. Best book on public speaking. A must-read if you do this at all. Great concrete advice and personal tales.

title: The Profit Zone
author: Adrian Slywotzky
context: The Profit Zone - by Adrian Slywotzky Recommend it: 4/10. Date read: 2009-10-14. Dryer but deeper prequel to the great “Art of Profitability” book, also recommended here. Start with that one. Only read this if that one fascinated you.

title: Never Eat Alone
author: Keith Ferrazzi and Tahl Raz
context: Never Eat Alone - by Keith Ferrazzi and Tahl Raz Recommend it: 4/10. Date read: 2009-07-26. A good book that's mostly about networking, but also some general business smarts. Definitely read if you need more work being social.

title: What Would Google Do?
author: Jeff Jarvis
context: What Would Google Do? - by Jeff Jarvis Recommend it: 4/10. Date read: 2009-03-05. Great think-piece about lessons learned from Google's approach to things, and how they might approach different industries like airlines, real estate, education, etc.

title: Speaking of India
author: Craig Sorti
context: Speaking of India - by Craig Sorti Recommend it: 4/10. Date read: 2008-09-30. Required reading for anyone doing business in India, with detailed analysis of cultural and communication differences. Example: in India a lack of emphatic “yes!” means “no”. Teaches Westerners to adapt to this.

title: Richard Branson
author: Losing My Virginity
context: Richard Branson - by Losing My Virginity Recommend it: 4/10. Date read: 2008-06-01. Autobiography of his life from childhood through 2004. Interesting how he was always over-leveraged and how that drove him forward. Amazing how he negotiated Necker Island from £3 million down to £180k.

title: Cambridge Language Surveys: Chinese
author: Jerry Norman
context: Cambridge Language Surveys: Chinese - by Jerry Norman Recommend it: 3/10. Date read: 2026-05-03. 80’s book about Chinese, helped me understand how simplified Chinese writing came about: not as much top-down as bottom-up formalizing of shorthand and cursive that had been in use for centuries.

title: Travelling While Black
author: Nanjala Nyabola
context: Travelling While Black - by Nanjala Nyabola Recommend it: 3/10. Date read: 2026-04-20. Thoughts on human rights, race, gender, travel, inequality, tribe, home, visas, poverty, Kenya, Africa, and Bessie Head.

title: Maintenance of Everything, part one
author: Stewart Brand
context: Maintenance of Everything, part one - by Stewart Brand Recommend it: 3/10. Date read: 2026-03-03. Because I loved his book “How Buildings Learn”, I expected a more philosophical look at maintenance, but it’s mostly a deep dive into a few specific examples of boats, guns, and cars.

title: You Will Not Stampede Me
author: Bryan Caplan
context: You Will Not Stampede Me - by Bryan Caplan Recommend it: 3/10. Date read: 2026-02-17. Tiny blog posts about non-conformity. I love his writing in general, but these were topics that I’d already read his writing on before, or too out of my realm (like academic life) to be interesting to me.

title: At the Existentialist Café
author: Sarah Bakewell
context: At the Existentialist Café - by Sarah Bakewell Recommend it: 3/10. Date read: 2026-01-05. More like a memoir of her re-discovery of existentialist writers. Interesting but because of it, less educational than I wanted.

title: Half Known Life
author: Pico Iyer
context: Half Known Life - by Pico Iyer Recommend it: 3/10. Date read: 2025-09-14. Travels in Iran, Jerusalem, Kashmir, Broome. Talks with tour guides. Writes some insights.

title: Belt and Road
author: Bruno Maçães
context: Belt and Road - by Bruno Maçães Recommend it: 3/10. Date read: 2025-06-26. Exploring implications of a vague Chinese plan to interconnect infrastructure with most countries. Written 2016-2018, making future predictions about times now passed. I got a few insights.

title: All the Ghosts in the Machine
author: Elaine Kasket
context: All the Ghosts in the Machine - by Elaine Kasket Recommend it: 3/10. Date read: 2024-12-28. Wonderful subject: how to handle digital data after death. But focused almost entirely on Facebook and Google, and the bureaucracy in place of those big social media corps.

title: Guru’Guay Guide to Montevideo
author: Karen Higgs
context: Guru’Guay Guide to Montevideo - by Karen Higgs Recommend it: 3/10. Date read: 2024-05-25. Basic information in preparation for travel.

title: From Rebel to Ruler
author: Tony Saich
context: From Rebel to Ruler - by Tony Saich Recommend it: 3/10. Date read: 2024-04-10. One hundred years of the Chinese Communist Party. I thought there would be more cultural insights but it was mostly just historical facts.

title: Questions Are the Answer
author: Hal B. Gregersen
context: Questions Are the Answer - by Hal B. Gregersen Recommend it: 3/10. Date read: 2024-01-04. I wanted to learn more about asking better questions in personal life, but this ended up being mostly about asking questions in a business team, with lots of stories of his consulting in big businesses.

title: Anchored
author: Lucas Skrobot
context: Anchored - by Lucas Skrobot Recommend it: 3/10. Date read: 2023-09-10. The author is one of my favorite people, and I liked his East-vs-West cultural insights, but they were too few, since the book wasn’t really about that.

title: The Barbell Prescription
author: Jonathon M. Sullivan
context: The Barbell Prescription - by Jonathon M. Sullivan Recommend it: 3/10. Date read: 2023-09-01. Weight lifting, strength training for people over age 40. Some good tips.

title: UAE Culture Shock
author: Gina Crocetti Benesh
context: UAE Culture Shock - by Gina Crocetti Benesh Recommend it: 3/10. Date read: 2023-05-30. Overview of United Arab Emirates culture from an outsider who lived there for many years.

title: UAE Culture Smart
author: John Walsh
context: UAE Culture Smart - by John Walsh Recommend it: 3/10. Date read: 2023-05-08. If you are interested in United Arab Emirates, but know nothing about it, this is a good starter book. Very short quick introduction.

title: Mistakes Were Made (But Not by Me)
author: Carol Tavris
context: Mistakes Were Made (But Not by Me) - by Carol Tavris Recommend it: 3/10. Date read: 2022-12-04. We are wired for self-justification. We create fictions that absolve us of responsibility, restoring our belief that we are smart, moral, and right — a belief that often keeps us on a course that is dumb, immoral, and wrong.

title: Useful Belief
author: Chris Helder
context: Useful Belief - by Chris Helder Recommend it: 3/10. Date read: 2022-11-30. Self-fulfilling beliefs. Focus on what is helpful to believe about a situation, and it can become true. Some good ideas, told in a weird way of a fictional guy getting on an airplane to speak at a conference.

title: The Question Behind the Question
author: John Miller
context: The Question Behind the Question - by John Miller Recommend it: 3/10. Date read: 2022-01-21. A quick little read with one point: We should take full responsiblity. Instead of asking blaming questions like “Why is the service here so terrible?” ask empowering questions like “What can I do?”

title: The Tao of Wu
author: RZA
context: The Tao of Wu - by RZA Recommend it: 3/10. Date read: 2022-01-21. Founder of Wu-Tang Clan tells his tale and philosophy. But while the symbolism of Shaolin inspired him, it wasn’t communicated in this book as anything useful. Still, could be a good for a below-the-surface reflection for how this mental association turned into better actions for him.

title: Writing to Learn
author: William Zinsser
context: Writing to Learn - by William Zinsser Recommend it: 3/10. Date read: 2021-09-04. Part memoir, part writing instruction, but mostly just examples of good writing from different disciplines. The point is that writing well about a subject helps you learn it, and reading great writing about a subject makes a huge difference. But too much of the book were just examples that I didn’t find useful for my needs.

title: Skip the Line
author: James Altucher
context: Skip the Line - by James Altucher Recommend it: 3/10. Date read: 2021-06-26. I love James Altucher for his unique vulnerable thinking. Many of his books have fresh surprising ideas. Unfortunately, this book has less than his others. But it’s a fine overview if you’re feeling lost and need motivation.

title: Lying
author: Sam Harris
context: Lying - by Sam Harris Recommend it: 3/10. Date read: 2018-02-10. A tiny booklet, like a long article, about why lying is bad. Not as many insights as I expected.

title: The Daily Stoic
author: Ryan Holiday
context: The Daily Stoic - by Ryan Holiday Recommend it: 3/10. Date read: 2016-12-10. This would be great as a daily email, and I think that's how it was intended. But as a book, with 365 tiny chapters, each point feels too shallow. Like reading nothing but blog posts for days. Still, great thoughts inside, so go to dailystoic.com to subscribe to that daily email.

title: Leading an Inspired Life
author: Jim Rohn
context: Leading an Inspired Life - by Jim Rohn Recommend it: 3/10. Date read: 2016-08-24. Great beginning. Absolutely adored the opening of this book, about discipline. Loved it so much it made me jump out of bed and go work for a few hours in the middle of the night, totally inspired. But then the rest of the book was ridiculously generic, with the occasional great sentence. Still, worth getting for that first chapter alone.

title: The Drunkard’s Walk: How Randomness Rules Our Lives
author: Leonard Mlodinow
context: The Drunkard’s Walk: How Randomness Rules Our Lives - by Leonard Mlodinow Recommend it: 3/10. Date read: 2016-04-12. I thought it was about the philosophy of randomness, but turned out to be about the math of probability. Might read again some day when in the mood for that.

title: How I Found Freedom in an Unfree World
author: Harry Browne
context: How I Found Freedom in an Unfree World - by Harry Browne Recommend it: 3/10. Date read: 2016-01-03. Some fun "fist in the air" thoughts on freedom, from 1973. Includes related thoughts on parenting and honesty.

title: The Sense of Style
author: Steven Pinker
context: The Sense of Style - by Steven Pinker Recommend it: 3/10. Date read: 2015-09-01. Advice on being a better writer. But compare to the book “On Writing Well”, also listed here. That one is punchy and immediately useful. This one is a more verbose, in-depth analysis of the use of language. Also useful, but, well, I wish it was shorter.

title: A More Beautiful Question
author: Warren Berger
context: A More Beautiful Question - by Warren Berger Recommend it: 3/10. Date read: 2015-07-07. A fine book, but maybe because I've been around professional creatives instead of corporate-types for most of my life, I already knew this subject too well, so it wasn't very useful to me.

title: Make It Stick
author: Peter Brown
context: Make It Stick - by Peter Brown Recommend it: 3/10. Date read: 2014-12-20. Great core point: that effortful learning - not easy - is more effective. Also the importance of self-testing as a learning tool.

title: The Power of No
author: James and Claudia Altucher
context: The Power of No - by James and Claudia Altucher Recommend it: 3/10. Date read: 2014-11-01. Quite scattered book, but inside the mess was a nice reminder of the importance of saying no to anything that doesn't serve you well.

title: How to Learn and Memorize French Vocabulary
author: Anthony Metivier
context: How to Learn and Memorize French Vocabulary - by Anthony Metivier Recommend it: 3/10. Date read: 2014-04-08. Only interesting if you haven't read anything else about the “loci” / “memory palace” method of memorization. Had almost nothing to do with French. Obviously made from copy-n-paste with his other books about German, Spanish, Russian, etc. Just change a few words, and voila! New ebook.

title: The Checklist Manifesto
author: Atul Gawande
context: The Checklist Manifesto - by Atul Gawande Recommend it: 3/10. Date read: 2011-12-25. Like Malcom Gladwell, a book that could and should have been an article, but puffed up with 200 pages of supporting stories, mostly great detailed tales of his surgeon experiences where a checklist would have come in handy. Here's the book in one sentence: You should make checklists for any complex procedures or decisions.

title: Hiring Smart
author: Pierre Mornell
context: Hiring Smart - by Pierre Mornell Recommend it: 3/10. Date read: 2011-08-07. Good advice on hiring. No big surprises, but some useful tips.

title: A Gift to My Children
author: Jim Rogers
context: A Gift to My Children - by Jim Rogers Recommend it: 3/10. Date read: 2011-07-15. A nice short book of unconventional wisdom, mostly about investing.

title: Pomodoro Technique Illustrated
author: Staffan Nöteberg
context: Pomodoro Technique Illustrated - by Staffan Nöteberg Recommend it: 3/10. Date read: 2010-01-11. Pretty cool technique of working in 25-minute chunks. Better to start with a simple article about it, then read the book after if you love it. I do, so far.

title: Causing a Scene
author: Charlie Todd
context: Causing a Scene - by Charlie Todd Recommend it: 3/10. Date read: 2009-08-18. Fun tales from the guy that invented Improv Everywhere. Not really educational as much as just fun, and I'm a huge fan of their “missions”.

title: Born to Run
author: Christopher McDougall
context: Born to Run - by Christopher McDougall Recommend it: 3/10. Date read: 2009-06-21. Gripping story of a man who was trying to find out why his feet hurt while running. This led him to the story of the Tarahumara Indians of Mexico’s Copper Canyon, the greatest distance runners in the world. If you like running, you’ll love this book! My favorite quote: “No wonder your feet are so sensitive. They’re self-correcting devices. Covering your feet with cushioned shoes is like turning off your smoke alarms.”

title: How to be a Billionaire
author: Martin Fridson
context: How to be a Billionaire - by Martin Fridson Recommend it: 3/10. Date read: 2009-04-23. Biographical look at billionaires from the last 200 years, and lessons learned from how they did it. Some lessons aren't really applicable to the rest of us, like changing government laws to protect your monopoly. But some are.

title: Enough
author: John Bogle
context: Enough - by John Bogle Recommend it: 3/10. Date read: 2009-04-23. Legendary investor, now 80, looks back with long-view wisdom on investing, living, and giving.

title: Reality Check
author: Guy Kawasaki
context: Reality Check - by Guy Kawasaki Recommend it: 3/10. Date read: 2009-03-08. Great collection of essays about entrepreneurship from his blog at blog.guykawasaki.com

title: Fooled by Randomness
author: Nassim Nicholas Taleb
context: Fooled by Randomness - by Nassim Nicholas Taleb Recommend it: 3/10. Date read: 2008-04-05. Mr Black Swan sure does love the sound of his own voice. Interesting thoughts on investing and misjudging randomness inside lots of blather.

title: The Obsolete Employee
author: Michael Russer
context: The Obsolete Employee - by Michael Russer Recommend it: 3/10. Date read: 2007-10-01. How to run a company without employees, but with a loose network of work-from-home freelance agents. Very instructive, but also good perspective like how until the industrial revolution, there were no employees: everyone was freelance.

title: Secrets of the Millionaire Mind
author: T. Harv Ecker
context: Secrets of the Millionaire Mind - by T. Harv Ecker Recommend it: 3/10. Date read: 2007-06-12. If you suspect that your mindset is holding you back from making more money, read this. Identifies and dissolves the mental baggage we've built up that believes money is evil and those who have it are greedy.

title: Execution
author: Larry Bossidy and Ram Charan
context: Execution - by Larry Bossidy and Ram Charan Recommend it: 3/10. Date read: 2007-02-12. In-depth look at the dirty discipline of getting things done in a large organization.

title: Reflections and Moral Maxims
author: François duc de La Rochefoucauld
context: Reflections and Moral Maxims - by François duc de La Rochefoucauld Recommend it: 2/10. Date read: 2026-09-02. Entertaining for the first few minutes, then you catch on to the formula of his little stupid sayings based on opposites. Then you notice his deeply misanthropic disgust of all people, especially women. Also this book has a weirdly verbose preface by the translator, almost as long as the contents.

title: Kingdom of Characters
author: Jing Tsu
context: Kingdom of Characters - by Jing Tsu Recommend it: 2/10. Date read: 2026-01-27. Since I’m learning to read and write Chinese, I thought this was going to go more into the history of the characters themselves, but it was about the technological innovations that enabled their adoption and distribution.

title: Create Your Own Economy
author: Tyler Cowen
context: Create Your Own Economy - by Tyler Cowen Recommend it: 2/10. Date read: 2025-10-28. Surprised me by being a book about autism. But it had some good points anyway.

title: Asian 21st Century
author: Kishore Mahbubani
context: Asian 21st Century - by Kishore Mahbubani Recommend it: 2/10. Date read: 2025-07-08. A collection of his essays around the subject of Asia thriving, but too often comparing with America, and rehashing his other book “Has China Won?”

title: Co-Intelligence
author: Ethan Mollick
context: Co-Intelligence - by Ethan Mollick Recommend it: 2/10. Date read: 2025-06-12. I was so excited to read this, hoping it would give new insights and expert tactics for getting more out of GenAI LLMs. But unfortunately it was almost nothing I didn’t know.

title: The Network State
author: Balaji Srinivasan
context: The Network State - by Balaji Srinivasan Recommend it: 2/10. Date read: 2025-01-09. It’s a great thought experiment: how to start a new country. Good core idea: God → State → Network. I was intrigued until it descended into long rants against America, like it was written only for Americans. I gave up after 100 more pages of that. I hope this idea is made vivid by a great movie/show.

title: The Four Agreements
author: Don Miguel Ruiz
context: The Four Agreements - by Don Miguel Ruiz Recommend it: 2/10. Date read: 2024-06-15. Hm. I liked it the first time I read it in 2006. This time? Seems like a lot of generic blah blah, trying to declare it to be deep and powerful by calling it Ancient Toltec Wisdom™.

title: Islam and the Future of Tolerance
author: Sam Harris and Maajid Nawaz
context: Islam and the Future of Tolerance - by Sam Harris and Maajid Nawaz Recommend it: 2/10. Date read: 2024-01-23. A dialogue between Sam, a famous atheist, and Maajid, former radical. Like listening to a podcast about Islamism, jihadism, extremism, fundamentalism. I admire that they did this, but the perspectives that interested them the most did not interest me.

title: Cyprus Culture Smart
author: Constantine Buhayer
context: Cyprus Culture Smart - by Constantine Buhayer Recommend it: 2/10. Date read: 2023-09-15. If you want to better understand Cyprus, this little book helps explain some basic context, culture, and history.
